en: Preface to the Study of the Pure Land I often sigh that in this Sahā world there are immeasurable sufferings; within the cycle of birth and death, there is no fixed place of rest.

Having barely attained a human body, in an instant one follows the retribution of evil and sinks into the underworld. How fortunate it is that the World-Honored One’s compassionate vow is profound, specifically launching the ferry of mercy to save us.
Sunk in the mire, he spontaneously proclaimed the Dharma of holding the Name, desiring to cause all sentient beings to emerge from the dust of the world.
From his distant ancestors, he propagated it throughout the Eastern Land; at Mount Lu, he established a community to cultivate the Pure Land, and countless noble practitioners were all reborn there.

Later generations of worthies followed in his footsteps. Alas! The True Dharma has met with decline; disciples are in great numbers, yet they delight in contending for cleverness. One must simply reflect...
The mind of Amitābha is manifest; yet, refusing to accept this, one instead seeks for someone else. One knocks with the very tile used to rattle the door, only to strike one’s own mother.
How pitiable—to gallop backward along the narrow goat-paths! To say that there is only the Mind and no other land—such a false view is even more lamentable.
Fortunately, the Master’s power shall employ both compassion and wisdom to distribute the medicinal Dharma universally to relieve the maladies of the age.

Every single character and phrase is entirely refreshing, enabling one to swiftly transcend the mundane without exception. This divine jewel is a treasure beyond measure, resembling the celestial net reflecting a thousand lights.

How could the capacities of beings be divided into high or low? Each receives according to their own lot, yet all that is received is extraordinary. (The "divine jewel" refers to the collection of writings compiled by the Master.)

Extremely timely, this opens up the perfect understanding. Those who study pure karma should contemplate it deeply. Alas! By what karmic affinity have I encountered a luminous teacher? A single word has brought me clarity, curing my blindness and folly.

(Ying formerly delighted in holding the Name, yet I was ashamed that I lacked essential instruction. I was graced by the Master’s demonstration of the analogy of an infant falling into water and crying out urgently for its mother to save it; my frantic seeking was instantly stilled, and I was deeply moistened by the milk of the Dharma.
I only wish that the Jewel of the Dharma may abide forever in the world, so that everyone may study according to it and receive its grace.
On the Mid-Autumn Day of the year Yihai, the first year of the Guangxu era of the Great Qing, I, Zhao Ying, a junior disciple from Zhenyang,
reverently burned three incense sticks from my arm and prostrated myself while inscribing this before the Baoen Gate at Fayuan Hermitage.

For the sake of my friends, I have inscribed this "Essentials for Rebirth" upon the reliquary niche.
Recalling the Buddha’s grace, I shed tears; rejoicing in having received such a direct path, I lament my former errors and excesses.
The Name is the Original Vow; by holding the Name, one naturally attains it. This is the essential strategy for holding the Name.
Upholding the Name is as weighty as upholding the mouth; upholding the Name shall surely produce its echo. Upholding the Name subdues delusion;
the three karmas are perfected through cultivation. There is a verse for my own portrait, titled "Small Reflection," which serves as a poignant spur to self-examination.
I briefly praise his profound kindness and wail before the Buddha.
Piercing my finger to draw blood and vent my feelings, I sincerely recite the Buddha’s name; may this recitation comfort and advance me as the three karmas operate in unison.
While circumambulating the Buddha, I have composed these essential verses on the importance of holding the Name.
I vow that all sentient beings shall be born in the Lotus Land. These words of exhortation for retreat practice are intended to warn against what is not in accord with the Way.

Indeed, those sentient beings with heavy karmic obstructions find it difficult to accomplish the path; they are most pitiable.

In ancient times, the person from Kunshan developed a mind of true reality, cast aside miscellaneous worldly activities, and single-mindedly upheld the Buddha’s name, desiring to seek liberation from suffering in this very life. Who would have known that within the practice of upholding the name...

Furthermore, you give rise to various views of a self and take pleasure in broadcasting your own understanding. Having not practiced literary composition in the past, you now particularly delight in producing disorderly works;

is this not a form of perversion? Moreover, the sublime scriptures of the ancients are piled up like mountains, yet you compose further works upon them—this is truly like discarding a *maṇi* jewel to seek out pebbles.
You ruin your own true virtue and become an object of ridicule for the wise. All of this stems from [your attachment to] birth and death.
Consequently, he was disturbed by this māra. In the spring of the Guiyou year of the Tongzhi era, while engaged in his writings, he fell gravely ill;
only then did he realize that his obstacles to the Path were not slight. Regretting that the wild horse of his mind was difficult to restrain, he made a vow to discipline it.

Later, because old vows remained unfulfilled, he became confused and deluded in all matters, still committing transgressions. He realized that if he did not repent, these would inevitably become evil obstructions. Therefore—
On the Buddha’s birthday in the year of Yi-hai (1835), I reverently burned nine incense sticks from my own arm, confessed my transgressions, and made a solemn vow, saying:
"To compose writings without merit is truly shameful; I lament that my greedy heart is difficult to restrain. I vow never to do so again in this life;
to do so again would be to act as a rebellious son of the Buddha. Thereupon, I recorded my self-reproach and the ugliness and clumsiness of my entire life.
I have compiled this into a single volume for my own reference and constant self-exhortation; it is titled *The Student of the Pure Land*.

It is that which I have studied through strenuous effort, following the power of faith. (Faith means believing that the Buddha’s grace is bestowed upon one, whereby one is able to enter this Dharma-gate; thus, one suddenly forgets one's own vulgarity and various shortcomings.
Alas, for several years I have been restless day and night for the sake of this single matter, exhausting my mind and laboring my strength to an indescribable degree of suffering.
Therefore, upon the completion of this manuscript, I reverently burned forty-eight incense sticks from my arm as an offering to Amitābha Buddha, making this vow:
"May I, by virtue of these roots of goodness derived from following and studying [the teachings], soon behold the Buddha and hear the Dharma;
may I soon be able to preach the Dharma to benefit sentient beings. Written on a summer day in the year of Yihai (1875), during the first year of the Guangxu era, by the junior student Gukun.
The Ritual for Reciting and Contemplating the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* at Ba’en Pass of Fayuan Hermitage. At the age of forty-eight.
Compiled briefly by the junior student Gukun, following ancient precedents, after the ritual for reciting and contemplating the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* taught by the Buddha.

The Sūtra says: The Buddha told Śāriputra, "If there are good men or good women who hear this sūtra and accept and uphold it, or who hear the names of the various Buddhas, they shall all be protected and remembered by all the Buddhas, and they shall all attain non-retrogression from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, Śāriputra..."
"You all should faithfully accept my words, as well as those spoken by all the Buddhas. Therefore, know that this sutra is inconceivable;

it is the essential heart-essence of all Buddhas and the fundamental framework of the Dharma-gate. Its phrasing is concise yet its principles are clear; its text is brief yet its matters are complete.
Every single word is the true refuge for the practitioner; every single word is the wondrous contemplation of the practitioner. However..."
Upon merely hearing its name, one immediately attains the stage of non-retrogression and is protected and remembered by all Buddhas; how much more so for those who receive, uphold, and recite it!
Before I left the household life, I first obtained this sutra; however, it was only upon reading the *Yaojie* (Essential Commentary) that I came to realize its profound and subtle nature.
From that time forth, I made a vow to receive and uphold it, aspiring to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. Indeed, the adornments of the Pure Land are exceedingly profound and subtle, and are not—
Within the reach of the mental power of ordinary beings, only this scripture—concerning both the primary and secondary aspects of the Pure Land—is somewhat accessible to the common mind;
it is a sublime expedient means by which Amitābha’s great vows receive and guide those of the lowest capacities. Therefore, it is said:
"Sentient beings who hear this should make a vow to be born in that land. Why is this? Because one shall be able to assemble together with such superior and virtuous people.

In one place, this exhortation for ordinary beings of the lower realms to attain rebirth so as to dwell together with the noble ones of the higher realms—this exceptionally superior Dharma gate depends entirely upon this.
That all Buddhas offer their praise is solely for this reason. I respectfully follow the Master Shi’s ritual procedures for receiving and upholding [this teaching].
I have briefly compiled this ritual for visualization and recitation, based on firm faith and aspiration. Following the general purport of the sutras, it is divided into twelve sections.

Recite the liturgy according to these sections while silently visualizing the scenes as described in the sutra. Facing west with reverence, as if [the Buddha] were present before one’s eyes, though the primary and secondary marks may not yet be clearly perceived, one’s faith and aspiration will already be genuine.
By thus single-mindedly holding the Name, both emptiness and existence will be simultaneously revealed.
Both principle and phenomena are fully contained herein. Śākyamuni and the Buddhas of the ten directions have raised their voices in unison to exhort you toward faith;
how can you not exert yourselves? You should know that this sutra is truly the family letter from the Land of Bliss. The adornments of that land are none other than one’s own ancestral possessions.
Amitābha, our compassionate father, has been waiting for us for a long time; if we practice this with resolve to seek rebirth, not even ten thousand oxen could turn us back.
In the autumn of the Jisi year of the Tongzhi era, this was recorded at Tiantai Jiaoguan in Jingjiao Temple.
(When a practitioner performs visualization during worship, they first kneel before the Buddha, burn incense, join their palms, and say:)
May these clouds of incense smoke pervade the worlds of the ten directions, making offerings to all Buddhas, to this Dharma difficult for the world to believe, and to all those of supreme goodness.
May they universally perfume all sentient beings, causing them all to resolve upon Bodhicitta. (Then rise and prostrate to the Buddha.)

With single-minded devotion, prostrate yourself and pay homage to Śākyamuni Buddha, the Original Teacher who, in this Sahā world of the five turbidities and evil age, has preached this Dharma so difficult to believe.
(Bowing down, silently contemplate a passage from the sutra, beginning with: "Śāriputra, as I now praise the inconceivable merit of the Buddhas," and continuing until: "this is most difficult.")

With single-minded devotion, prostrate and pay homage. Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, extend the broad and long tongue to exhort and praise the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the Western Quarter (from "Śāriputra, just as I now praise the inconceivable merit and benefits of Amitābha Buddha," down to "the Sūtra on Being Protected and Mindfully Kept by All Buddhas of the Upper Quarter").
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, whose light and lifespan are immeasurable and who universally gathers all living beings.
(Śāriputra, what do you think? For what reason is that Buddha named Amitābha? From here down to "ten kalpas have now passed.")
With single-minded devotion, pay homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, who guides one at the moment of death through the upholding of his name.
(Śāriputra, it is not by means of few roots of goodness... down to ...one should make a vow to be born in that land.)
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to the Western World of Ultimate Bliss. Now, you and all others should make the vow that everyone shall be reborn there.
Amitābha Buddha. (Śāriputra, if there be anyone who has already made the vow... down to "...shall be born in that land.")

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to and praise the *Sūtra on the Inconceivable Merits Praised by All Buddhas and Protected by Their Mindfulness*, as well as all the Honored Dharmas of the ten directions and the three periods of time (from "Śāriputra, what do you think? For what reason is it called... down to "...and all that has been spoken by the Buddhas").

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the World of Ultimate Bliss in the western quarter, to Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and all the noble and virtuous beings, as well as the assembly of pure Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas like a vast ocean.
(Furthermore, from "Śāriputra, that Buddha has immeasurable and boundless śrāvaka disciples" down to "all gathered in one place.")

With single-minded devotion, pay homage to the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the western quarter. Beneath the trees where the spiritual birds dwell, one hears their sounds and maintains right mindfulness.
[The passage from] "Furthermore, Śāriputra, in that land there are always various wonderful birds of diverse colors" down to "accomplishing such adornments of merit" is concluded.
With single-minded devotion, pay homage to the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the western direction, where golden ground is profusely adorned with flowers as offerings to the Buddhas,
and where all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas [furthermore, Śāriputra, in that Buddha-land, celestial music constantly plays, down to the Adornments of Merit].
With single-minded devotion, pay homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas within the precious pavilions inside the lotus ponds of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
(Furthermore, Śāriputra, in the land of Ultimate Bliss there are ponds made of the seven treasures... down to "...adorned with merits.")

With single-minded devotion, pay homage to the Western World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), where there is no suffering whatsoever and only various joys are experienced by all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.
(At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder... down to "...for this reason that land is named Ultimate Bliss.")
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and all the great Bodhisattvas; to Śāriputra and all the great Mahāśrāvakas;
and to all the holy assemblies of the ten directions and the three periods of time. (From "Thus have I heard" down to "together with the great assembly of immeasurable devas.")
Having performed the ritual visualization, kneel and recite one scroll of the *Amitābha Sūtra* and the *Wǎngshēng Zhòu* (Dharani for Rebirth) three times.
Then offer praise, saying: The body of Amitābha Buddha is golden in color; His marks and signs and radiance are peerless. The white tuft of hair curls like five Mount Sumerus;
His deep blue eyes are as clear as the four great oceans. Within his light, countless billions of transformation Buddhas appear, And hosts of transformed Bodhisattvas likewise...
Boundless. Through forty-eight vows, he delivers sentient beings, causing those of all nine grades to ascend to the other shore.
*Namo* to Amitābha Buddha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful. (Recite the name of the Buddha as many times as your strength permits, then cease.
*Namo* to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. *Namo* to Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva. *Namo* to the Pure Great Ocean.
The assembly of Bodhisattvas (ten recitations each), having completed their mindfulness, dedicate the merit and make this vow: "Disciples,
having recited the name of the Buddha Amitābha, whose merits are true and real,
we pray that you will compassionately grant us your acceptance, bearing witness to our repentance and our aspirations."
All the evil karmas I have created in the past, Arising from beginningless greed, hatred, and delusion,
Produced by my body, speech, and mind— I now confess them all. May I,
when the time comes for my life to end, Be completely cleared of all obstacles.
Having beheld that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face, I shall immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
All the roots of goodness I have now cultivated, I dedicate them all without exception;
May all sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm Together be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Taking refuge in the Buddha, may all sentient beings realize the Great Way and give rise to the unsurpassed mind.
Taking refuge in the Dharma, may all sentient beings enter deeply into the treasury of the scriptures, their wisdom becoming like the ocean.
Taking refuge in the Sangha, may all sentient beings lead and harmonize the great assembly, free from all obstacles.

Regarding the ritual for bowing to and visualizing the Noble Assembly (*āryasaṃgha*): as for how long one should practice each day, it may be according to one's capacity. However, the two periods of morning and evening must by all means not be omitted.
At the final session, once the recitation of the Buddha’s names is complete, one should kneel upright before the Buddha with palms joined. First...
Recite the Forty-Eight Vows. Recite again the names of Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the assembly of the Pure Ocean. Make vows and dedicate the merit.
It is even better to prostrate while reciting the Forty-Eight Vows. One should join the palms and settle the mind, speaking as if before the Buddha:

With single-minded devotion, prostrate before Amitābha Buddha, the Greatly Compassionate, Greatly Merciful, Greatly Vowed, and Greatly Powerful Guide and Teacher of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.

(Having finished this recitation, bow down. Contemplate the First Vow: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, there should be any in my land who are hell-beings, hungry ghosts, or animals, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.

Prostrate for the second time. Contemplate the Second Vow in the same manner. Prostrate before Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the great assembly of Bodhisattvas (three prostrations each). [Recite the vows and dedication as before.]
(Thus ends the Homage and the Three Refuges).
Verse from the Amitābha Sūtra:
From this western direction lies the City of Bliss; Amitābha preaches the Dharma even now. Seven layers of trees are covered with pearls.
A net of freedom and ease, severed from the wheel of suffering.
Within the ponds of the seven treasures, the waters of merit overflow; the lotuses are fragrant and pure, their bases of solid gold.
The stairways on all four sides are joined with lapis lazuli, and the multi-storied pavilions are fashioned of agate.
They walk back and forth upon the ground of pure gold; heavenly music frequently plays the sounds of the Dharma. Wondrous flowers that please the mind fill their robes;
they ascend at will to the Buddha-lands of other directions.
Spiritual birds emerge from the nets upon the trees, producing profound sounds; day and night they constantly proclaim the names of the Triple Gem.
Upon seeing forms or hearing sounds, right mindfulness arises, and the fruit of the path to Bodhi is spontaneously accomplished.

The body of perfect marks and signs, in which ten thousand virtues are harmoniously integrated, radiates light that universally illumines and gathers all sentient beings. His lifespan is inconceivable, equal to the life-span of humanity;
therefore, he is titled the Venerable Immeasurable One.
Countless śrāvakas and noble beings always dwell in one place as if of a single class; when ordinary persons arrive here, none ever regress.
Those who hear this should make a vow to be born there.

The adornments of the environment and its inhabitants are peerless; how could they arise from the mere cultivation of mixed merits and virtues? By holding the Name with a single, undistracted mind, the transformation Buddhas will come to welcome one, and the fruit of the Way will be realized.

In this defiled and evil Sahā world, this sutra is preached; with a broad tongue reaching the ten directions, it encourages all living beings. You should believe it with earnest attention and harbor no doubt;
its adornment of merit will be accomplished in every thought-moment.
The merit of this sutra is wondrous and inconceivable; the Golden Mouth [the Buddha] earnestly exhorts its upholding. Should one merely hear its name, they will be protected by the Buddhas;
such a person shall never regress from Bodhi.
If you wish to go to Amitābha’s City of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī), you should now vow to transcend birth and death entirely. Such a perfect and sudden teaching is inconceivable;
it rests solely upon the depth of one's own power of faith.
The karma and defilements of sentient beings in the five turbidities are deep; the path cannot be accomplished without upholding the Name.
Our Original Teacher performed this most difficult task, as all Buddhas together extend their broad tongues.
In this *Sūtra Spoken by the Compassionate One*, he specifically employs skillful means to gather those of the three faculties. Mañjuśrī and Śāriputra both listened and received it;
we, each and every one, shall practice it accordingly.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Amitābha Sūtra) is the most essential scripture of the Pure Land tradition. Having encountered it through a karmic affinity, one must not treat it with levity.
This hymn is composed entirely based on the essential points within the sūtra; it is not the result of mere conjecture.
Readers should contemplate it with a tranquil mind and not perfunctorily, for only then will they understand that Śākyamuni and the Buddhas of the ten directions act for the sake of our suffering.
It afflicts sentient beings; yet through compassion, it rescues and relieves them. Such is its benevolent virtue. How could those who possess the Buddha-nature fail to believe this?
I only pray that my fellow practitioners will uphold this with all their might. Relying upon this merit, may we be born early in the Western Land.
An Exhortation to Recite Sūtra Verses:
During the Liang Dynasty, there was a monk named Daozhen who lectured on the Mahāyāna sūtras for several decades. Although he saw ships sailing westward, he was unable to go;
this was solely because he had not yet recited the Amitābha Sūtra.
The Ritual for Entering Contemplation and Performing Liturgy upon Going to Sleep, compiled by the junior scholar Gu-kun Zungu based on the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*.
It states: The Buddha addressed Ānanda and Vaidehī: "Listen attentively, listen attentively! Well done!"
"Reflect upon this. I shall explain for you in detail the method for removing suffering and affliction;

you should remember and uphold it, and explain it in detail for the great multitude. When these words were spoken, Amitāyus Buddha stood poised in mid-air, with the two Great Beings, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, standing in attendance at his left and right, their radiance blazing intensely.
It cannot be fully described; even the hundreds of thousands of colors of Jāmbūnada gold cannot be compared to it.

For this reason, I am firmly convinced that Śākyamuni Tathāgata and Amitābha Buddha, while in their stages of practice (*bhūmi*), together made vows of compassion and together opened the gates of *saṃgrahavastu* (the means of attraction) and *vidhāraṇa* (the methods of subduing). Thus, as soon as our Original Teacher spoke the Dharma for removing suffering and affliction, he—
The Buddha then manifested his body, fully adorned with all its majesty.
Vimalakīrti and the others felt their joy for the Pure Land deepen ever further, while their revulsion toward the defilements of this world grew ever more intense.

In truth, although Vimalakīrti and the others had not yet performed the visualizations, they were profoundly weary of the suffering and afflictions of the Sahā world and deeply rejoiced in the compassion of Śākyamuni, our Original Teacher.
This is merely an instruction. The Great Master Zhi said: "If one wishes to be definitively reborn in the Western Land, one must possess both the practice of aspiration and the practice of revulsion.
How true these words are! They truly capture the sublime secret for Lady Vaidehī’s rebirth.

Therefore, we know that for sentient beings with heavy karmic obstructions who wish to cultivate the visualization of the Buddha, it is essential only to have deep faith in Śākyamuni’s method of subduing.
By speaking thus, one gives rise to weariness with [samsara] and, single-mindedly admiring the virtue of Amitābha’s compassionate reception, one gives rise to joy.
Bowing toward the west with a sincere heart, the Buddha will surely know of this from afar; at the time of death, he will certainly come to welcome and guide you.

In truth, by currently bowing toward him in accordance with the sutras, the Buddha has already been moved to approach you; it is only because sentient beings have heavy obstructions that they do not perceive it themselves.

The Way of Resonance is such that its principle is necessarily so. For this reason, relying on the words of the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* and following the model of Master Shandao, I have briefly compiled the Ritual for the Eight Contemplations and Recitation to be performed at bedtime.
As for "worship," it means worshipping the Buddha’s body, which manifests with sovereign mastery through supernatural powers and transformations according to one's wishes.
As for "recitation," it means reciting the teachings of our Original Teacher, which analyze and explain the Dharma to sever all suffering and affliction.

This is the Dharma. Those who cultivate pure karma must follow this; only then will they know that the vow-power of the two Buddhas transforms sentient beings in unison, and that their compassion is such as this.
As for the ritual for the nine grades, it was composed by me, a person of humble views and fallible intellect, as a supplement.
Because even those of the lowest grade of evil can obtain the benefit of addressing the Buddha, I pay homage to it to urge myself on against my deep obstacles and shallow merit.

This is merely to dispel the spirit of despondency that fears one may fail to attain rebirth. In the winter of the Gengwu year of the Tongzhi era, this was noted at the Dokbulhyeon Hall of Jingiao Jangsa Temple.
(When a practitioner has completed a day’s ritual service, they should perform this practice before the Buddha.)
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Original Teacher Śākyamuni Buddha, who provides detailed explanations of the methods for eliminating suffering and affliction in this Sahā world.
(Prostrate; while bowing low, recite the verse:)

The nature of the worshiper and the object of worship is empty and quiescent; the mutual resonance of cause and response is inconceivable. My this place of practice is like a jewel of Indra, within which the shadow of Śākyamuni Tathāgata appears. The shadow of my body now appears before the Tathāgata, seeking to transcend suffering as I prostrate at his feet.
With single-minded devotion, pay homage to Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.

Abiding upon a precious lotus flower above the waters of the lake, he manifests a body sixteen feet tall, with a form of true golden color. His halo is brilliantly radiant and penetrating; within this halo dwell immeasurable transformation Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
(The verse for visualization says:)

The nature of the worshiper and the object of worship is empty and tranquil; the mutual resonance of cause and response is inconceivable. My place of practice is like a jewel of Indra, within which the reflection of Amitābha Buddha appears. The reflection of my own body appears before Amitābha, so that, seeking rebirth, I may prostrate at his feet.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Buddha Standing with a Celestial Crown upon the Waters of the Pond in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss,
and to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara (in the verse of visualization, change "Avalokiteśvara" to "the manifestation of Avalokiteśvara").
With single-minded devotion, pay homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta (in the verse of visualization, change "Mahāsthāmaprāpta" to "Śrīprabhāsa"),
who dwells in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss upon the waters of the pond, with a jeweled vase atop his *uṣṇīṣa*.

With single-minded devotion, prostrate yourself and pay homage to those who are born in the highest grade of the highest level in the World of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*). Recite the scriptures and cultivate loving-kindness so that the three minds are fully developed.

[Prostrate to all the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas. (After the prostration, silently contemplate the text of this chapter, etc.—the subsequent sections follow this pattern. Alternatively, one may simply direct one’s sincere homage toward them without contemplating the scriptural text.)

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage. To those Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who are born by the middle grade of the superior lot in the World of Ultimate Bliss, who understand the ultimate truth and whose minds are not shaken—homage to them!

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage. As for those Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who attain birth in the highest grade of the lower level in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, they merely give rise to the unsurpassed, pure mind of the Way.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas who are born in the middle grade of the superior rebirth in the world of Ultimate Bliss, who practice all the precepts, and who are free from all faults and afflictions.

With single-minded devotion, pay homage! Those who maintain the precepts and dignified conduct for one day and one night shall be reborn in the middle grade of birth within the world of Ultimate Bliss among the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who are born in the middle-to-low grade in the World of Ultimate Bliss, who filially support their parents and practice benevolence and compassion in the world.

With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, those born in the highest of the lower grades are greeted by the Buddha of Many-Evil-Names and the three sages, as well as by the various Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.

With single-minded devotion, I prostrate. Those born in the middle grade of the lower level in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, who have violated the precepts but heard of the Buddha when the fires of hell were extinguished and the Holy One approached—[to all] these Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage. Even those of the lowest of the low grades reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, or those who have committed heinous crimes, attain transcendence by invoking the Buddha’s name ten times.
To all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas, [I pay homage].

Having completed the prostrations and contemplation, kneel with palms joined and recite the "Contemplation of the Nine Grades" from the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (the Contemplation of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; one must consult the *Xigu xingyi* and *Lianzong biyu*).
Recite until reaching the passage: "One shall sit at the site of enlightenment and be born into the family of all Buddhas.

With a sincere heart and all one's strength, recite ten breaths for "Namo Amitābha Buddha," ten times each for "Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva," "Namo Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva," and "Namo the Assembly of Pure Great Ocean Bodhisattvas. Then, make this vow:

I, disciple [Name], am currently an ordinary person caught in the cycle of birth and death. My karmic obstructions are profound and heavy; as I transmigrate through the six realms, my suffering is beyond description.

Now, having encountered a spiritual friend, I have been able to hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and the merits of his original vows. With single-minded devotion, I invoke his name and pray for rebirth in his land.
May the Buddha, out of compassion, not forsake me, but look upon me with pity and take me into his care. I, disciple [Name], do not understand...
The Buddha’s body, with its marks and signs and radiant light— may the Buddha manifest these so that I may behold them,
as well as the assembly of Bodhisattvas such as Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and the pure adornments, radiance, and wondrous marks of that world,
so that I may see them all clearly. (Having prostrated three times before the Buddha, return to the quarters to rest.)
The Verse on the Chapter of the Nine Grades of Contemplation:
Recite the Mahāyāna sutras while fully giving rise to the three minds; practice the six mindfulnesses along with a compassionate heart. By means of these merits, seek rebirth there;
when the Buddha’s holy ones arrive here in boundless numbers, they will welcome you (the highest grade of the highest birth).

The Mahāyāna does not slander the clarity of cause and effect; furthermore, it explains the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) within the sutras. The three sages personally approach and a thousand buddhas follow;
simultaneously extending their hands, they welcome one back to go [to the Pure Land] (Middle Grade, Middle Birth).
If one merely arouses the bodhicitta and seeks the Land of Ultimate Bliss, at the moment of death the Three Holy Ones will come to welcome them.
Five hundred transformation Buddhas will arrive simultaneously, all praising the practitioner for having aroused the supreme mind (the lower grade of the highest rebirth).
Practicing the various precepts without any transgressions, one vows for rebirth through these roots of goodness. At the moment of death, Amitābha comes to offer praise and instruction;
having left the household life, one will certainly be liberated from all suffering and distress. (The Superior Birth of the Middle Grade)
For one day and one night, they upheld the various precepts; their majestic deportment was flawless and their merit profound.
Thus, they were graced by that Buddha’s coming to praise them, and by following the words of the sutra, they attained rebirth (in the middle grade of the middle birth).
One who is able to practice filial piety and benevolence, and finally encounters a great and virtuous teacher, hears the exposition of Amitābha’s vast power of the original vow;
in the time it takes to extend or contract one's arm, they arrive at the Lotus Pond (Middle Grade, Lower Birth).

A fool, shameless, commits many evils; yet at the moment of death, he is able to recite the name of that Buddha. The Three Sages suddenly arrive in accordance with his thought, consoling him by saying:
"Your sins are extinguished; I have come to welcome you" (The Superior Birth of the Lower Grade).

A person who has violated the precepts is about to fall into hell when they suddenly encounter a spiritual friend who praises the Great Name. Upon hearing this, their boundless sins are immediately extinguished;
the fierce fires are thus dispelled, and the Three Sages appear before them. (Middle Birth of the Lower Grade)

The offenses of the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds are extremely grave; yet, if at the moment of death one encounters a virtuous friend who instructs one to recite the name of Amitābha ten times, one will immediately see a lotus flower come to welcome them (the lowest grade of the lowest birth).
Regarding the verses on the nine grades: they merely praise the causes for practice and the conditions for rebirth.
As for those of the lower three grades, they were originally all evil persons who, at the moment of death, briefly cultivated the cause of reciting the Great Name of the Buddha.

Consequently, they immediately encountered the condition of the Buddha coming to welcome them. How could there be a more perfect and sudden (sudden-enlightenment) method than this? Within the ocean of Amitābha’s vows, even the wicked are embraced.
The compassionate grace and virtue of the Buddha extend even to this degree. Therefore, one should know that the only thing to fear is not reciting the Buddha’s name;
there is no need to worry about failing to attain rebirth in the Pure Land. Even a wicked person who practices for a mere moment at the time of death still feels the Buddha’s arrival;

how much more so for one without evil who has recited the Buddha’s name throughout their entire life—how could the Buddha not come to their rescue at the end? Thus, the Great Master Zhiwei said: "When the signs of the fiery chariot appear, a single thought..."

If one repents, one can still attain rebirth; how much more so for those who cultivate the power of the pure path through the熏修 (xūnxiū—perfuming and cultivation) of precepts and meditative concentration, whose merit shall not be in vain.
These nine grades of practice constitute the great gateway of skillful means for sentient beings with heavy obstructions to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Those who exclusively perform pure deeds must not fail to bring them to maturity. I, Gu Kun, have fortunately obtained the benefit of this chapter;

I first conceived the thought that I might accomplish [enlightenment] within a single lifetime. Therefore, upon concluding these verses, I reverently burned nine incense sticks from my arm as an offering to the virtuous persons of the nine grades.
I vow that I may swiftly escape saṃsāra and quickly ascend to the lower grade (because my mind was often distracted while reciting the Buddha’s name).
Gu Kun, unworthy and backward as I am, have traveled the path to the West to resolve my doubts and advance myself.
Yet, being foolish, inferior, and possessed of a fiercely burning defiled mind, I am unable to aspire toward any of the various Dharma gates.
The single practice of merely holding the Name is the most supreme expedient; it gathers in even the most wicked, rebellious, and foolish people.
Master Xingcan said: "That Buddha’s power of vows is uniquely transcendent, leaving behind neither the five heinous crimes nor the ten evil deeds.

If one’s faith, aspiration, and holding of the Name are not deficient, in future years one will surely be entrusted to a lotus flower. Inspired by this, I made a vow to exclusively hold the Name, yet I was helpless [to avoid obstacles].
Habitual tendencies from past lives are particularly strong, and the mind-monkey is difficult to restrain.

I have respectfully composed forty-eight verses based on the name of Amitābha Buddha and the essential words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, to serve as a whip for my progress. Furthermore, with deep faith in the Buddha’s vows, I resolve to seek birth in the Pure Land.
As the Patriarch Shandao said: "There is only the shortcut practice; simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. Therefore, I take the Western Path as my guide.
In the *Deciding Doubts and Advancing Strategies* (*Lù jué yí cè jìn míng*), it is asked: "The Wise One’s *Treatise on the Ten Doubts* asks:
'I wish to resolve to seek rebirth in the Western Land, yet I do not know what practices one should perform or what should serve as the seed for attaining birth in that land.

Answer: Those who wish to resolve to be born in the Western Land must possess two types of practice to certainly attain birth there: first, the practice of weary detachment (*yànlí xíng*); second, the practice of joyful aspiration (*xīnyuàn xíng*). Adhere to these."
I respectfully set forth these two gates of delight and aversion as the preliminary guides for the path.
Praising the Buddha arouses delight;
the Teacher of the Sahā World opens the gate to the Pure Land—most difficult to encounter and rare, most sudden and most perfect.
The Buddhas of the ten directions, with their broad tongues, proclaim in unison, earnestly praising and exhorting sentient beings:
"The Guide to Ultimate Bliss possesses boundless light and lifespan; through his compassion, he gathers and sustains all.
Those of the nine grades ascend together, as all ten thousand sutras point the way and myriad sages follow. Transcending the three realms horizontally—this alone is the one gate."

Self-Exhortation: Contemplate with revulsion that the affairs of birth and death are of great consequence; impermanence is swift. Once one loses this human body, it is difficult to regain it for ten thousand kalpas.
Though we temporarily dwell among humans, we have always resided in hell; our retributive suffering is boundless, originating from the three poisons.
Bound by the entanglements of affection, one entangles and binds oneself; if one does not give rise to a mind of revulsion, when can one be liberated?

The Dharma gates are immeasurable and truly difficult to master; with single-minded recitation of the Buddha’s name, one will certainly be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss—this is the path for pressing forward.
The single phrase "Amitābha" was spoken with ultimate compassion. Upon hearing this dharma so difficult to believe, one should vow to be born in that land.
The single phrase "Amitābha" is protected and remembered by all Buddhas. Those who hear its name and uphold it shall all attain non-retrogression.
The single phrase "Amitābha" is proclaimed together by all six directions; extending his broad and long tongue, he exhorts all sentient beings.
The single phrase "Amitābha" was spoken with earnest urgency by Śākyamuni: "All should believe my words, as well as those of all the Buddhas."
A single phrase of Amitābha: its radiance illuminates the ten directions, universally gathering all who recite his name to ascend together to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
A single phrase of Amitābha: his lifespan is inconceivable, and that of all his people is likewise identical, without any difference whatsoever.
A single phrase of Amitābha is replete with wondrous adornment; those of supreme goodness gather together, and for those born there, there are no conditions for regression.
A single phrase of Amitābha—those who believe should make the vow; by upholding the Name, one will be reborn there, which is itself a source of great merit and virtue.
A single phrase of Amitābha is embraced by the vast vows of Dharmākara; were one not to be reborn in the Pure Land through ten recitations, I would never become a Buddha.
A single phrase of Amitābha—his power of vow is truly immeasurable; even when the fires of hell appear at the moment of death, ten recitations lead one to the Western Land.
A single utterance of "Amitābha" possesses the power of immeasurable merit. Like a great stone placed upon a boat, one will certainly not sink.

A single utterance of "Amitābha" eliminates the sins of immeasurable kalpas; if merely hearing the name brings liberation from suffering, how much more so for those who recite it with earnest mindfulness!
A single phrase of "Amitābha" possesses the deepest affinity for those in the Age of Dharma’s Decline; other practices are difficult to accomplish, whereas this alone transcends all others.
A single phrase of "Amitābha" is the diverse skillful means of all Buddhas. Those who wish to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing should recite it with single-minded devotion.
A single phrase of Amitābha is most highly extolled in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra; Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and all others alike vow to be reborn in that land.
A single phrase of Amitābha is proclaimed in thousands of sūtras and ten thousand śāstras: between that Buddha and us there exists a great karmic affinity from past lives.
A single phrase of "Amitābha": Huiyuan knew its profound mystery; its merit is supreme and its progress most easy. Reciting the Buddha’s name is the foremost practice.
A single phrase of "Amitābha": Zhiyi bequeathed this final word; even the wicked and rebellious attain rebirth there, so pure conduct is never in vain.

One phrase of "Amitābha": Shandao elucidated the two gates; those who practice exclusively will all go [to the Pure Land], while those who perform miscellaneous practices find it difficult to be reborn there.
One phrase of "Amitābha": Chengyuan practiced without ceasing; he exhorted and transformed ten thousand people, all of whom cultivated in this same manner.
A single phrase of Amitābha: Fǎzhào asked Mañjuśrī that this one dharma-gate alone is most suited to the capacities of beings in the final age.
A single phrase of Amitābha: Shàokāng vowed never to change his resolve; using coins to entice young children, he universally exhorted them all to recite the Buddha’s name.
A single phrase of Amitābha: through wisdom and awakening, one ascends to the first stage. Discerning that there is the Pure Land, ten thousand who practice, ten thousand depart.
A single phrase of Amitābha: this is the supreme instruction of Ciyun. The ten recitations are most essential; one should develop resolute faith in rebirth.
"A single phrase of Amitābha": Xingchang established the Pure Conduct Society; the worthies joined together to open wide the gate of nianfo.
"A single phrase of Amitābha": Lianchi possessed right view; at the time of his death, he bestowed compassionate instructions, requiring only that one recite with sincerity.
A single phrase of Amitābha—Master Youxi expounded its wondrous principle: this mind of mine that recites the Buddha’s name is the perfectly interfused essence of the Dharma-realm.
A single phrase of Amitābha—Master Ouyi deeply realized its meaning: even one who is to attain Buddhahood in their next life can still depart while carrying over their karmic hindrances.
A single phrase, "Amitābha," is spoken with firm and dense resonance according to the occasion. It is a poignant statement of the three great essentials;

first, the urgency of delighting in the Pure Land and loathing this world. A single phrase, "Amitābha," was spoken by Xingcan in his poetic exposition: these six characters encompass heaven and earth, requiring no three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

A single phrase of "Amitābha": through this, one attains thorough awakening; thus he left behind his final instruction. With a single recitation of the Buddha’s great name, a single portion of his physical marks and signs appears.
A single phrase of "Amitābha": it has been transmitted from patriarch to patriarch. When the Buddha’s name encounters a distracted mind, that very distracted mind becomes a Buddha.
A single phrase of Amitābha encompasses the entirety of the Tripiṭaka; it brings the lowly down to earth and the sages up above—this Dharma is beyond compare.

A single phrase of Amitābha universally benefits all sentient beings, causing them all to attain the stage of non-retrogression; the nine grades are distinguished according to their individual capacities.
A single phrase of Amitābha—its resonance is inconceivable. Even those who invoke the Buddha’s name with a distracted mind shall all ascend to the land of An-yang.
A single phrase of Amitābha—how joyful is the Buddha’s encouragement! Even those who harbor doubts or feel regret shall be born within the borderlands of that realm.

A single utterance of "Amitābha" allows one to transcend horizontally across the five realms of existence; if ten recitations can still bring accomplishment, how much more so when reciting ten million billion times!
A single utterance of "Amitābha" plants a lotus as soon as it is spoken; if every thought remains inseparable from the mind, its blossoms will remain fresh at all times.
A single phrase of Amitābha, without relying on the power of expedient means; if the mind of mindfulness is undisturbed, one shall see the Buddha as soon as the lotus blooms.

A single phrase of Amitābha, entirely dependent on the intensity of faith and vow; though there may be much distraction in reciting the Buddha’s name, all nine grades of rebirth are encompassed within it.
One phrase of Amitābha—his compassionate heart to rescue and protect is most urgent; even those who have committed the ten evils and the five heinous crimes are all enabled to be born in that land.
One phrase of Amitābha—his benevolent virtue is incomparably deep; it causes me to plant roots of goodness until I reach the stage of succeeding to Buddhahood.
A single phrase of "Amida": the Buddha-realm arises through causes and conditions. Though his traces have not yet left this Sahā world, his spirit dwells within the lotus flower.
A single phrase of "Amida": the path ascended is infinite and boundless. It is easy to travel, yet no one does so; how lamentable, how truly a pity!
A single phrase of Amitābha is the unsurpassed Great King of Physicians; he can cure all illnesses. To lack faith is truly lamentable.
A single phrase of Amitābha is the great compassionate vessel across the sea of suffering. If everyone is willing to board this boat, each and every one will reach the Western Land.
A single phrase of Amitābha—its divine power is unfathomable. Even a magpie calling the Buddha’s name shall be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
A single phrase of Amitābha—the compassionate Father of myriad virtues. May I and all sentient beings swiftly proceed to the Land of Peace and Joy.
An Inscription for Resolving Doubts Regarding the Path:
Our Buddha, the Tathāgata, the most honored among all the sages, has bestowed extraordinary skillful means to perfectly encompass those of the three capacities.
By merely upholding his name, one may ascend to the Buddha-land; with a single voice he reaches all, and throughout ten lands he proclaims it in unison.
Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra both vow to be reborn here; Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna all revere and follow this path.
Ten thousand sages and myriad saints enter this same gate together. Those who harbor doubts and lack faith fall into the fiery pits of hell.
The ocean of the Buddha’s merit is deep and vast, unfathomable; like all rivers flowing toward the sea, all beings are gathered within it.
The Name of Amitābha accomplishes myriad virtues and universally delivers all living beings, enabling them to ascend together to that land.
Even those on the verge of falling into fierce flames find their suffering instantly stilled by a moment’s invocation; those already entered into hell depart upon hearing the Name.
These manifestations of responsive resonance cannot be fully described, yet if one is willing to turn the mind, the ocean of suffering can be crossed at once.
On the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the eighth year of the Tongzhi era, at the West Chamber of the Tiantai Teaching and Contemplation Hall,

he made a vow to uphold [the practice] by burning twelve incense sticks from his own arm as an offering to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* spoken by the Buddha. He further vowed to recite six fascicles of the sutra every day and to invoke the name of the Buddha.

Chanting sixty thousand times as the limit for one's entire life, he reflects thus: "Our original teacher, Śākyamuni, out of compassion for us, has opened the gate of rebirth in this world of five turbidities.
Our compassionate father, Amitābha, out of compassion for us, has made the sixty-eight great vows to adorn the Pure Land.
The Buddhas of the six directions, out of compassion for us, have extended their broad and long tongues in unison."
He offered words of exhortation and praise. Thus we know that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions cherish sentient beings as a mother remembers her child;

from the beginningless kalpas, they have never for a moment abandoned them. Yet, out of self-reproach for their own folly in abandoning their father and fleeing, they have remained submerged in saṃsāra for many kalpas, unaware of their plight and feeling no sorrow.
Moved by grief, they wept with flowing tears and composed these verses:
Recalling the West, my tears drench both eyes; I grieve that for many kalpas I have been burdened by the Compassionate Honored One.
Though his adorned merits are all perfected, alas, the ocean of karma in this Sahā world is deep.

The Master’s correspondence from the Land of Bliss is fundamentally universal; the Buddhas support one another so that the path remains unobstructed. The Compassionate Father leans upon his gate, constantly harboring anxious thoughts;
how pitiable is the deluded child, so utterly muddled.
The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is originally my own hometown; having drifted for many kalpas, I had long since forgotten it.
Fortunately, the Benevolent One conveyed this message, so that I finally know my Compassionate Father is in his hall at home.
The moment I think of Sukhāvatī, my heart is filled with sorrow; this Saha world is truly loathsome, with its myriad forms of suffering. My Compassionate Father has long held me in his thoughts;
from now on, I shall never again wander through these sights.
Regarding the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on Amitābha) which exhorts one to uphold the sutra and practice mindfulness of the Buddha:

it is the ultimate compassionate heart of our original teacher Śākyamuni and the Buddhas of the six directions, who, for the sake of us sentient beings of this defiled and evil age, have described that pure buddha-land and earnestly exhorted us to go there. Amitābha...
Amitābha Buddha, by the power of his great vows, receives and leads those sentient beings in the Sahā world who practice mindfulness of him. This dharma gate is supreme and wondrous;
its praises can never be exhausted. One should faithfully accept all these sincere words from the Golden Mouth.
One fascicle of the *Amida Sūtra*: the great compassionate heart of the Buddhas of the ten directions. Relying solely on this path, one transcends birth and death;
the merit of myriad virtues is accomplished in the snap of a finger.

Of the eighty-four thousand sublime Dharma gates, the single phrase of Amitābha is most honored. From all ten directions, they extend their broad and long tongues, together praising the Western Land and exhorting rebirth there.
Out of profound compassion, why do I so earnestly exhort you to recite the name of Amitābha? The wind and waves of this Saṃsāric ocean of suffering are perilous;
within the white lotus flower, there is much joy.

The praise for his lifespan and radiance is inexhaustible; he gathers all sentient beings throughout boundless worlds. If one can, for even a single thought-moment, give rise to devotion and reverence, one shall ascend to the Palace of Ultimate Bliss from the vast stages of existence.

Tiantai thoroughly realized the source of his own mind; he personally beheld the events at Vulture Peak as if they were still present. Seated, he never turned away from the west, constantly reciting the Buddha’s name;
at the end of his life, he simply invoked the conditions for the Land of Bliss.

The master of the Yongming school emerged above the multitude of worthies; principle and phenomena are harmoniously integrated as the mirror of mind hangs suspended. Myriad virtues are cultivated together to return to the Pure Land;
yet nine out of ten err in what they call "empty Chan."
The legacy of Shandao’s teachings is transmitted through the ages; he exhorted people to practice nianfo with single-minded devotion. Know that this is the direct path of cultivation:
the single phrase of Amitābha is the most supreme condition.

Holding jade within my breast, my vow for the Golden Terrace remains firm; though the Silver Terrace appears, I shall not follow its conditions. Throughout my life, I have practiced nothing but the truth:
morning after morning, I recite the name of Amitābha fifty thousand times.
The single phrase of Amitābha is the King of Dharmas; Though distracting thoughts swirl in confusion, they do not hinder it.

Ten-thousand-mile clouds may obscure the blazing sun, Yet its residual radiance remains everywhere throughout the human world. (The *Yaojie* states: "The excellence of the Pure Land refers to being born with one's karma still attached into the Shared Realm of Purity; this relies entirely upon the power of that Buddha’s light and vows.
Distracting thoughts flying about are truly pitiable; No thousandfold schemes can dispel them. How could one know that within a single phrase of Amitābha?

The Buddha does not sever ordinary sentiments to enter the womb of sainthood (Tianru says: "With deep faith in the Buddha's power, even those possessed of afflictions and defilements can attain rebirth; thus there is the teaching of 'transcending horizontally while carrying one's karma'). That Buddha’s vows and practices during his causal stage were sublime;
he adorned and perfected a precious land for us. By merely reciting the Name ten times, one transcends to birth there;

how could the enjoyment [of that land] ever diminish by a single hair? (Dharmakara’s vow states: "If those who wish to be born in my land do not achieve it through as few as ten recitations of my name, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.")
How truly extraordinary is this Dharma gate! Even an evil and rebellious ordinary person can reach the stage of the sages;

when the fires of hell appear before them, they rely on ten recitations to sit upright upon a precious lotus throne at the moment of death. (Quan’an said: “As for the Samādhi of Buddha-recitation, it makes no distinction between the wise and the foolish, the noble and the lowly, nor does it consider the duration or the nature of one’s past deeds—whether good or evil.

It takes only resolute faith as its standard. Thus, even those of the lowest class, through ten recitations at the end of life, attain rebirth in the Pure Land and transcend to Buddhahood in a single instant. This is what Yongming called the inconceivable power of the Buddha: ‘How marvelous! Such a thing has never existed before in the history of the world.’”)

This is the "Verses on Mindfulness of the Buddha through the Immediate Mind," a commentary on Master Youxi’s *Yuanzhongchao*. It holds that the environment and inhabitants of Sukhāvatī constitute wondrous existence (*miaoyou*), while single-mindedly reciting the name constitutes true emptiness (*zhenkong*).
Without the subtle true emptiness, one cannot realize the wondrous existence of Sukhāvatī; and without the subtle wondrous existence, [true emptiness remains unmanifested].
This is able to reveal the empty vacuity of this very mind. Combining these two meanings, he composes a verse: "Mind itself is the Buddha;
the sound of each invocation of the Buddha's name is emptiness merging with emptiness. The dependent and the primary are perfectly present therein: A single bright moon appears in a thousand rivers;
Vividly clear, it leaves no trace."
The lands of the heart-enclosing ocean are boundless; the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is vividly present before one's eyes.
As soon as one fixes the mind upon a single invocation of Amitābha, one’s own body now dwells within the lotus of the Jade Pond.
In every thought-moment, Amitābha; in every thought-moment, the mind. With every sound, awaken the person who is one's original nature.
One should know that the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power is profound as an ocean of vows, gathering in and sustaining all living beings.
A single phrase of Amitābha, a single rosary; bead after bead reflects one another as precious light unfolds. Mutually containing and mutually pervading, it is inconceivable;
thus one transcends the sea of suffering horizontally to dwell in Ultimate Bliss.

Expressing My Sentiments on the Practice of Buddha-Recitation I have often observed that certain practitioners of Zen disparage the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation, claiming it is merely for the sake of the ignorant masses.
Moved by these views, I have set down my humble reflections here. Written at Hoguk-sa Temple by the Baesa Spring in the Jisi year of the Tongzhi era.
Do not disparage the practice of nianfo as being for the ignorant; even the enlightened must enter this school.
A single phrase of Amitābha is the total manifestation of reality—what need is there to seek a separate "master"?
The single phrase of Amitābha is the profound and wondrous Chan; it is the sincere word spoken by the Buddhas of the six directions.
To seek the meaning of the West beyond this is to wander abroad for fifty years (the fifty years symbolize the five realms of existence, as stated in the Lotus Sūtra).
Reciting Amitābha’s name with hands clasping beads—how does this differ from picking up a flower and smiling?
When one casually perceives the face of non-arising, the splendors of Sukhāvatī are seen to be none other than oneself.
There are no more complex mechanisms than this: simply recite the name of Amitābha with sincerity.
What is the meaning of the cypress tree in the courtyard regarding the West—what is this six-character Great Name?
In every thought-moment, contemplate Amitābha; in this state of awakening and stillness, mountains, rivers, and the great earth are no longer obstructed.
Boundless lands appear within it, and other Buddhas likewise emerge from the mind’s perception.
Amitābha is moment by moment serene and alert; that Buddha is vividly present as my own mind. When the Pure Land manifests, one’s original nature appears;
self and other are not separated by so much as a single speck of dust.
I have thought of Amitābha for but a few autumns; Amitābha has thought of me with vows that never cease.
Regardless of whether one's karmic offenses are light or heavy, it is sufficient simply to hold his name to go and roam in his land.
Morning and night I call upon Amitābha; my heart grows weary with longing and tears flow ever more. The eight sufferings press upon me with piercing intensity;
I know not what day I shall leave this Saha world.
How can one endure such heart-rending sorrow? With every cry, I weep and call upon the Elder Amitābha.
Having drifted and sunk through birth and death for many kalpas, may I now at last cross over the river of craving.
The mind-monkey and will-horse are most difficult to still; they have galloped through vast kalpas until this very day. Even in quiet mindfulness of Amitābha, one must not yet rest;
from now on, one must keep count with clear precision.
Transmigrating through birth and death is most cause for concern; one must urgently seek the path and practice cultivation. When reflecting upon every dharma, the mind finds no resonance;
only the Name of Amitābha perfectly accords with it.
A single invocation of the Buddha’s name encompasses all myriad virtues; why need one leave this place to seek elsewhere?
If one can simply maintain mindfulness in every thought without forgetting, the boundless ocean of the teachings is gathered within these six characters.
Reciting the Buddha’s Name:

The Teacher of the Sahā World bears the title Śākyamuni; His skillful means for universally saving all beings are profound. He preached the Dharma in five periods, distinguishing the sudden and the gradual;
Guiding according to capacities, he leads those lost from the ford of delusion.
The sentient beings of the final age are truly pitiable; though the King of Physicians has appeared, they lament their lack of karmic affinity. May you deign to bestow a single drop of true nectar;
once it enters the mouth, it can heal ten thousand ailments.
The sea of suffering in this Sahā world is as ceaseless as a wheel; suffering departs and suffering arrives, never resting. Death in suffering and birth in suffering are true sufferings;
the blade-mountains and sword-trees are even more profound in their agony.
Supreme bliss and leisure, beyond compare; those who linger there are all sages and worthies.
With golden-hued forms and infinite lifespans, they walk upon jeweled grounds as celestial music resounds.
My mind is vast and wondrous, beyond measure; the adornments of Sukhāvatī are my native home. In every phrase Amitābha calls out to me as "Mother";
come quickly and lead me into the jeweled hall.

The compassionate heart of that Buddha is immeasurable; he launches a vessel of mercy upon the bitter sea of Sahā. He constantly thinks of the wayward sons boarding the ship to depart, so that each may together return to the land of Ultimate Bliss.
Uttering one great name and crying out once, I cry every morning toward the Great Compassionate Honored One:
"If I do not return home this time, when shall I ever escape from the six realms?"
Uttering one great name and taking a single step, one is constantly treading the path home. Alas, the wayward son does not turn his head;
all day long he is busily preoccupied, always turning his back on his father.
Sitting facing west, visualize the pond and pavilion; the Pure Land appears vividly above the roof. It is regrettable that throughout the day it is constantly interrupted;
this is entirely due to not having practiced in past lives.
Gazing afar at the Land of Ultimate Bliss, I contemplate the compassionate countenance; it appears vividly and clearly before my eyes. It is a pity that throughout many lifetimes we have never met;
though I see you today, it is difficult to communicate.

The Western Pure Land is precisely the Mind-Only. To recognize Mind-Only, one must be reborn there; only by personally beholding the Jewel Forest and hearing the sublime Dharma proclaimed can one finally realize that every single thing is a treasure of the home.
The original-nature Amitābha, in his sixteen-foot form, sits majestically and upright upon a precious lotus throne.
When one clearly beholds him in that land after rebirth, he is none other than the old master of one's own house.
The *Anuttara-gambhīra-sūkṣma-dhyāna-mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* states: "If a person merely contemplates Amitābha, this is called the unsurpassed, profound, and subtle dhyāna.

When one perceives the Buddha through mental visualization with utmost sincerity, that is itself the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing. Thus, we know that dhyāna and purity are of one essence, and principle and phenomena are inseparable."
There is no difference between them. Yet I often see people of the world who recklessly distinguish right from wrong, clinging to Chan while slandering Pure Land. Is this not truly lamentable?
I have briefly set forth my humble thoughts merely to encourage myself.
A single phrase of Amitābha is the unsurpassed, profound, and wondrous dhyāna; it is itself non-arising and non-ceasing, as the Tathāgata personally proclaimed with his own mouth.
A single phrase of Amitābha is subtle, wondrous, most profound, and most secret; Vimalakīrti remained silent without speaking, and Faruo said he did not know it.
One phrase of Amitābha: the direct intent from the West. There is no need to ask how; simply go straight ahead. One phrase of Amitābha:
like the moon in the empty expanse of a clear pool, it appears with perfect clarity; ultimately, it is nothing other than this.
A single phrase of Amitābha: all of space vanishes; it pervades the worlds of the ten directions, yet cannot be found when sought.
A single phrase of Amitābha: all phenomena are entirely as they are; the vast ocean enters a single pore, and a mustard seed contains Mount Sumeru.
One phrase of Amitābha is the true and wondrous secret of non-arising. It is inherently perfect just as it is; to employ cleverness is, on the contrary, to become clumsy.
One phrase of Amitābha: the Mother of the Ten Directions yearns for her child. The deluded child seeks outwardly; when will his suffering ever cease?
A single phrase of Amitābha is the most supreme maṇi-jewel; it can fulfill all vows and swiftly bring about the unsurpassed path.
A single phrase of Amitābha is praised by all Buddhas; its merit is inconceivable—do not harbor even the slightest contempt for it.

Regarding the offering to the Buddha, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (The Fundamental Vow of Amitābha Buddha) states: "If sentient beings of the ten directions, upon hearing my name, should wish to be born in my land and yet fail to achieve this, may I not attain perfect enlightenment.
The *Amitābha Sūtra* further states: "It cannot be accomplished by means of few roots of goodness or merit..."
By these conditions, one may be born in that land. Upon hearing the teaching of Amitābha Buddha and upholding His name, one immediately attains rebirth there.

The *Sūtra of Contemplation* states: "When a rebellious and perverse being is on the verge of falling into hell at the end of life, if they are taught to recite the ten recitations of 'Namo Amitābha Buddha,' the fires of hell will instantly transform into lotus flowers. Furthermore, another sūtra says: "At the time when the Dharma is extinguished, the scriptures will remain entirely..."
There is none. One need only preserve the four characters of Amitābha Buddha’s name to deliver sentient beings.

Those who do not believe and instead slander it shall fall into hell and undergo all manner of suffering. Thus, we know that the name of Amitābha is the excellent medicine for emergency relief in the final age.
How much more so for one like me, Gu-kun, born in this final age with the heaviest karmic obstructions; having heard this—
The name of the Buddha must be received with the utmost reverence and put into practice with all one's strength.

Therefore, with a heart of supreme sincerity, he invited his pure friend Lien-gen to inscribe in large characters the six great characters of the Name, "Namo Amitābha Buddha," so that it might be venerated throughout his life.
Furthermore, the lay devotee Li Chongxi was moved to resolve his mind to gild [the scroll] and provide its mounting, thus completing it together with others.
With immeasurable joy and the utmost sense of gratitude, on the day of its hanging, he reverently burned nine incense sticks from his own arm and made this vow with a sincere heart:
I prostrate to Amitābha, the Compassionate Father through countless eons. This name of ten thousand virtues remains, flowing throughout the lands of the ten directions.
By what causes and conditions did I, in the past, encounter it this morning? Though it consists of but six characters, it is non-dual from my own being.
By this, I deliver sentient beings; my vow is profound and beyond compare. If one wishes to be liberated from suffering in this very life, there is no other way than this.
Therefore, I burn this arm as incense, making a great vow with utmost sincerity: until this present body of retribution comes to an end, I shall never cease to offer worship.
Having just unfurled it today, I kneel before it and recite with a solemn voice: "May it be that at the time of my life's end, I shall surely be joined with those of this day.
May I share the same destiny as the scribes and those who gilded the text; may we together attain rebirth in this very life, never to be parted throughout eternal kalpas."
May all who see or hear this each give rise to reverence; may each vow to uphold it; may each develop resolute faith.
By means of this merit, may they swiftly proceed to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, personally behold Amitābha Buddha, and just as the Buddha delivers all beings, so may they deliver them all.
A General Praise of the Dharma Gate of the Pure Land:
How wondrous! The minds of all sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature. Yet, without superior conditions, it remains hidden and concealed, never manifesting.
The Dharma King, the Unsurpassed Honored One, for the sake of this one great matter, has extensively established many skillful means to assist in manifesting the meaning of the Buddha-nature.

Those of small wisdom delight in small teachings and are unable to hear the Mahāyāna; thus, through skillful means, he preached the Small Vehicle, provisionally pointing toward the city of quiescent extinction.

Although the teachings of the Three Vehicles were expounded, they ultimately lead to the Buddha Vehicle. To enable easy accomplishment, he specifically opened the gate of the Pure Land and extensively propagated the Avataṃsaka teachings.
Great minds all leaped with joy; at the end, through the King of Ten Vows, they dedicated their merit toward rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
By the power of that Buddha’s great vows, he surpasses all lands in the ten directions; his adornments of the environment and its inhabitants are wondrously sublime, with merits beyond compare.
As soon as he utters a single sound, it is proclaimed throughout the ten directions. Such a wondrous Dharma-gate is the secret key to attaining Buddhahood.

If one can simply believe for a single thought-moment, one will certainly attain Buddhahood. When one recollects the Buddha in every thought-moment, in every thought-moment one has already become a Buddha.
The virtues of the Buddha are truly immeasurable; the mind’s praise cannot reach them. To speak even a few verses with all one's strength is like a hair soaking up a drop from the ocean.
May my fellow practitioners pass this on from one to another; by relying upon this most excellent condition, may they swiftly proceed to the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Amitābha Buddha stands by the lotus pond;
praise for the seven-jeweled ponds of the Land of Ultimate Bliss: within those ponds, the lotuses are beyond measure.
A great precious lotus flower surges upward in height; Amitābha Buddha dwells upon this flower, manifesting through supernatural powers a body sixteen feet tall.
His subtle and wondrously adorned golden form is radiant, with a halo so transparent it surpasses lapis lazuli; the emanated Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are all immeasurable.
The white tuft of hair is brilliant and pure, emitting radiant light that gathers in sentient beings to lead them back to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.
Avalokiteśvara stands to the left and Mahāsthāmaprāpta to the right; those reborn in the nine grades all gaze up in reverence.
The inconceivable spiritual power of that Buddha is praised by all the Buddhas of the ten directions.
I now call to mind the Buddha’s supernormal powers; May I, at the time of death, ascend to the other shore.

Longing for the West, may I rejoice by the banks of the Seven-Jeweled Pond, Listening to the sounds of the Dharma, Wandering freely upon the lapis lazuli steps and paths, And gazing up at the lotus flowers above the pond.
Within, it is entirely filled with those who recite the Buddha’s name in this Sahā world.
The multi-storied pavilions are composed of every kind of precious jewel; their radiance shines through clearly, utterly free from dust.
Here, the Dharma King expounds upon the profound principles, while all the superior and virtuous beings are filled with joyful smiles.
Celestial music resounds through the air day and night; heavenly flowers fall everywhere in profusion.
Those who walk upon the golden ground are all people making offerings of abundant flowers to the Buddha.

Layer upon layer of jeweled nets cover the groves of trees; the chirping of birds and the movement of the wind produce profound sounds. When sentient beings arrive here, their minds are peaceful and joyful;
whether sitting or reclining, they constantly praise the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
One should weary of the suffering of Sahā, for the three realms offer no peace, being like a pit of fire. Everyone dwelling here is scorched and consumed;
even if one performs good deeds to be born in the heavens, when merit is exhausted, one returns once more to the gates of hell.
Pleasurable matters have long been the conditions for suffering; yet fools are greedily attached to them with great intensity. For a brief moment, their wealth and nobility bring forth much karma;
after death, they must once again stand before the wardens of hell.

The physical body is a hollow illusion and a profound grievance; though one employs a hundred schemes to arrange it, all is in vain. The mutual encroachment of old age and sickness is especially fearsome;
at the time of death, the corpse swells and its stench permeates the heavens.

Affectionate attachments are enemies that cut to the very bone; they cause people to be constantly summoned by the King of Death. If one does not seek rebirth in the Peaceful Nurturing Land of that Buddha, how can one emerge from the cycle of the six realms?
Taking up this pen, I, the disciple Gukun,
reflect that from beginningless time until this present life, I have committed boundless transgressions and endured immeasurable suffering.

Now that I have obtained this human body, the three poisons still burn fiercely; in the future, I will certainly fall again into the three miserable realms, entering suffering after suffering with no prospect of liberation.
Only now do I realize this; it is tragic and painful. I take refuge in the Buddhas of the ten directions, who possess great merit and wisdom.
May you be able to rescue and deliver me and all sentient beings. If one's karmic resonance is not single-minded, the response of the Sages will not manifest.

Therefore, on this day, I make a vow with a sincere heart, respectfully burning two fingers and ten incense sticks from my crown, making offerings to the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the worlds of the ten directions who exhort and praise the Western Land.
I pray only that, through your great kindness and great compassion, you will together grant me your witness.
O Illuminator, take pity on me and accept me. With this single finger-offering, I make an offering to Śākyamuni Buddha, the Original Teacher of this Sahā world.
May I quickly abandon the suffering of the Sahā world and, until the end of the future, extensively deliver sentient beings so that they may likewise abandon this suffering.
With a single finger, I make this offering to Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.

May I swiftly attain the bliss of the West and, until the end of the future, extensively deliver sentient beings so that they likewise attain this bliss. Though space may come to an end, my vow shall be inexhaustible;
may all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm together perfect the All-Wisdom. May, in this present life, my roots of goodness increase and flourish. Do not...
Losing the causes for purity, at the moment of death, with body and mind in right mindfulness, their hearing and sight will be clear.

They shall behold Amitābha Buddha face-to-face, along with the assembly of Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta, who hold lotus pedestals in their hands to receive and lead them forth. In a single kṣaṇa, they will be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Upon the opening of the flower, they shall see the Buddha; immediately they will hear the Buddha Vehicle and suddenly awaken to the Buddha-wisdom, extensively delivering all beings.
Birth. Fulfilling the vow for enlightenment.
