Regarding the practice of forming a mandala and holding the name, the *Amitābha Sūtra* states: "From here, to the west, passing through a hundred trillion Buddha-lands, there is a world named Sukhāvatī."
It is blissful. In that land there is a Buddha named Amitābha, who currently dwells there preaching the Dharma. All those of supreme goodness gather together in one place;
there are no manifold sufferings, but only the experience of various joys. The power of that Buddha’s vows is inconceivable.

If there are those who hear of this and uphold his name, they shall all attain rebirth there at the time of their death, let alone those who follow the teachings shown by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
The Great Tongue Wheel. With earnest exhortation, the Teacher of the Sahā World offers repeated instructions; his words are fervent and poignant.
Though I am dull-witted and difficult to tame or subdue, the Buddhas look upon me with compassionate pity, and I shall surely attain accomplishment.

Therefore, relying upon the Buddha’s words, I have established a pure altar for seven weeks, performing prostrations and recitations during the six periods of the day and night, holding the name of the Buddha with single-minded devotion. Upon reaching each seventh day, I reverently burn [incense].
Twelve incense sticks of arm-incense were offered to the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* preached by the Buddha, as well as to all the Triple Gem.
He made vows as follows, according to the same finger-text.
Verses on the Sevenfold Repentance and Vow:
I bow my head to Amitābha, whose compassion and vows are inexhaustible. By sincerely invoking the Buddha’s name, his response appears at every moment.
Now, with a sincere heart, I look up to follow the instructions of all Buddhas; yet though I have recited the name for seven times seven days, I have not yet witnessed a response.
All this is due to the weight of past karma, which causes my mind to lack stability. My mindfulness of the Buddha is often distracted; alas, what a truly grievous malady!
Yet, relying on the Buddha’s compassion, even calling upon His name in distraction leads to sainthood. Therefore, I shall not abandon Him; my resolve shall remain firm for the rest of my life.
Now, once again lighting this arm-incense, I make offerings to the Sage among Sages. I repent for karmic deeds from beginningless time, that all may be swiftly purified.
I look up with aspiration to the Lotus Pond assembly—the Buddha and all the worthy sages—and pray that you will compassionately accept me and manifest your response at the moment of my death.
Attaining rebirth in this very life, the repayment of gratitude shall never end. When all sentient beings have become Buddhas, my vow will finally reach its consummation.
I universally pray that all virtuous friends may develop resolute faith in the Western Land; may all who see or hear of this each give rise to joy and celebration.
Preface to Reading the *Fuxuan*:

I am ashamed that my merit is meager and my obstacles many. Although I have left the household life, my mind does not adhere to the Way; thus, I wander through the cycle of birth and death—a state that is both lamentable and painful.
Though the Pure Land offers the expedient means of "horizontal transcendence," the ancient masters’ instructions on *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation) necessarily require...
Only through thorough investigation and clear understanding, with a single mind free from distraction, can one achieve success. This is no easy matter.

Although I have devotedly followed this path, alas, when I am reciting the Buddha’s name, my mind inevitably dwells on other things; despite all manner of suppression and restraint, it cannot be paused for even a moment—how lamentable!
Fortunately, by virtue of Amitābha’s power of vows, those of the nine grades are all gathered together, and the sufferings at the time of death...
Even if one is pressed by circumstances such that the mind cannot focus on the Buddha, if one recites the name ten times orally, one will still attain rebirth. The *Lotus Sūtra* states:

"Even a single recitation performed with a distracted mind leads to the attainment of the Buddha-way; if the merit of ten or even one such recitation is thus, how much more so for those who uphold, read, and recite it throughout their entire lives?
Relying on this, one should resolve their will. Whether one understands the meaning or not, whether the mind is focused or distracted, one should read [the sūtra] every day.
I recited the name of Amitābha Buddha sixty thousand times as provisions for the Pure Land; like a river flowing toward the sea, it shall certainly not be in vain.
Therefore, I inscribed the name of his dwelling as "The Studio for Reciting the Buddha's Name" (Dufu Xuan) and composed a verse to be attached to it.
Reciting the six-character scripture of the Western Paradise, one neither investigates the principles of Chan nor seeks the mind;
one simply relies on the proliferation of deluded thoughts and spends one’s entire life merely moving the lips.
I reflect upon Amitābha and find it deeply lamentable: though the mouth recites his name, the mind is scattered and cannot be subdued.
Relying on hearing that the Buddha possesses vows of compassion, the merit of ten recitations is perfected and one reaches that realm.

How painful! How painful! Truly painful it is! This karmic enemy of birth and death cannot be turned back. I have exerted all my strength in reciting the name of Amitābha, yet the mind-monkey rushes about and will not return.
How fortunate, how fortunate, truly fortunate! The gates of the Vows of Dharmākara are now wide open. Even those of extreme evil and folly can practice the Buddha-remembrance;
at the moment of death, they shall likewise be escorted to the purple-golden platform.
A Vow of Self-Exhortation:
From beginningless time, I have been tormented by greed and anger through hundreds of sufferings until this very day. Fortunately, I have felt the Buddha’s compassion and received his protection;
I vow to seek the Pure Land to benefit all sentient beings.
Having already heard the Buddha-dharma and become a monk, this is a rare and difficult encounter; such a matter is no light one.
I pray that you will soon join the assembly at the Lotus Pond, to extensively deliver sentient beings and repay the Buddha’s kindness.

I reproach myself for my foolishness and deep defilement by evil; though I seek the Buddha-dharma, I have achieved nothing in truth. To return empty-handed from the mountain of jewels is truly to be pitied;
I vow to contemplate Amitābha and escape the wheel of suffering.
I shall recite the name of Amitābha sixty thousand times daily; from this moment forth, I vow never again to be negligent.
I only hope to shorten my lifespan in Jambudvīpa and swiftly attain a body of the lowest grade in the Western Land.
Restrain worldly sentiments;
time passes swiftly and life is difficult to preserve. Each day one must guard against entering the gate of death. When guests arrive, do not speak of mundane affairs;
instead, recite the Buddha’s name without ceasing.
I know not when impermanence will descend; I must now mindfully call upon Amitābha to await my departure. Do not take offense at my casualness toward you gentlemen;
alas, the karmic obstacles of our kind are so deep.
The mind-monkey and will-horse cannot be stilled; one must establish a fixed schedule for reciting the Buddha’s name.
Set a morning quota of sixty thousand recitations, deeply ashamed of having failed to show respect to the noble guests above.

Listening to the teachings and practicing Zen are of no avail; being incapable, I should simply recite the name of Amitābha. You gentlemen of high station who come and go, please cease your inquiries;
have pity on me as you would an old woman.
The seven-day period of silence:
take seven days as the duration and do not seek anything outside. Face west and recite the Buddha’s name without ceasing. Time passes so easily; it is truly worthy of being cherished.
When honored guests arrive at the door, grant them leave to respond.
If you wish to achieve samādhi and be born early in the lotus, you must first sever external conditions for yourself. Speaking of right and wrong increases distraction;
therefore, do not speak a word for seven days.
Setting a fixed term, observe silence and recite the name of Amitābha; strenuously exhort body and mind, never letting them stray. The ocean of suffering is deep and vast, difficult to cross alone;
I vow to rely on the Buddha’s power to escape Saṃsāra.
The karmic conditions of my transgressions are truly lamentable; I have repeatedly encountered the calamities of war and fire.
I vow that from this life forward I shall escape birth and death, silently and single-mindedly seeking the King of Great Vows.
In daily practice, be careful with speech;
cultivate revulsion for birth and death and long for the Lotus Pond. Recite the name of Amitābha in the morning during the six periods. Human life is impermanent and truly fearsome;
even when facing guests, do not engage in excessive talk.

My daily recitation of the Amitābha Sūtra was not yet complete; when a guest arrived, do not be surprised that I remained silent and spoke no word. The matter of birth and death is so great that it is difficult to evade;
a dull horse must be struck with a stinging whip.

Ashamed of my verbal transgressions, I wish to silence my voice; yet fearing I might betray those of like mind who recite the Buddha’s name, I shall speak briefly of the matter of birth and death after midday.
As for matters of right and wrong or praise and blame, let not your lips be opened.

May my fellow practitioners look upon me with compassion and refrain from idle talk; I shall now speak of the conditions for the Western Pure Land. I feel ashamed that I have lacked learning until now;
in my deluded mind, I have thought only of the lotuses in the Jade Pond.
A Universal Exhortation to Mindfulness of the Buddha:
In the West there is a Buddha named Amitābha, Who receives and guides sentient beings out of the river of craving. All Buddhas proclaim this together; you should believe it with earnest attention.
By doing so, at the moment of death, you will avoid meeting King Yama.
To desire rebirth in Amitābha’s Pure Land and escape the fiery pit, one must rely on the power of both faith and vow, which must be equally profound. Know this:
the moment a single phrase is uttered, the lotus flower of Sukhāvatī has already blossomed.
When the five turbidities prevail, suffering increases daily; human faculties grow ever more debased and defilements ever deeper. In other approaches to learning the Way, accomplishment is difficult;
in the Pure Land, one transcends horizontally, making rebirth easy.
In the blazing house of fire, there is no door for escape; only in the West is rebirth exceedingly easy. Even an evil and rebellious ordinary person can achieve it through ten recitations;
there, the white ox reveals its entire body.
The gate to the Pure Land opens; the path is easy to traverse and easy to accomplish. Whether noble or foolish, all may rely upon it. By merely upholding the Name, all achieve success.
Dwelling together with those of supreme goodness, it is beyond compare.

The vow-power and radiant light of Amitābha embrace all boundless practitioners of nianfo. If one merely holds the name with an undistracted mind, the transformation Buddhas will surely come to welcome them at the moment of death.
The Pure Land of the West is beyond compare; there, one is born among the nine grades within the lotus ponds. In the Dharma-ending age, it is difficult to attain deliverance through other practices;
only by relying on this path can one escape from the depths of samsara.
Do not disdain the Dharma-gate of mindfulness of the Buddha; this single teaching can encompass all manner of capacities.
From the highest, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra, they have with one mind made vows and taken full refuge.
Having sat in meditation and realized the principle of perfect luminosity, how could one not wish to ascend to the Western Land? Master Jue entered meditative concentration for ninety days;
Amitābha made a hundred thousand vows to welcome those seeking rebirth.
It does not matter if you do not awaken to the mysteries of Chan; it is enough simply to focus your mind on reciting the Dharma King’s name.
Provided you attain rebirth in Sukhāvatī at the moment of death, you will suddenly open to the Buddha-wisdom, wondrous and immeasurable.

Thoroughly penetrating the meaning of the sutras is the spiritual root; one should properly rely on the sutras to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. A single volume of the Avataṃsaka encompasses the oceanic treasury;
may the King of Rebirth dedicate these merits so that we may behold the Compassionate Honored One.
To recite the name of Amitābha without being versed in the sutras is superior to possessing great intelligence and wisdom;
the six characters of the Great Name are the true Dharma-realm, universally encompassing the ocean of teachings and free from confusion.
When glory, splendor, wealth, and honor fulfill one's desires, even the "Western Land" is but a provisional name.
When the single breath does not return and one departs empty-handed, one stands alone and solitary before King Yama.
In poverty and hardship, you toil day after day; it is precisely now that you should turn your mind toward the Buddha. Your home in the Land of Ultimate Bliss is not far away;
you must return with haste—do not let the moment slip away.

The foolish who create karma will surely sink into the depths; those who recite the Buddha’s name will certainly behold the Buddha’s body. Since even those of the ninth grade—those who have committed the most heinous rebellious acts—are still gathered therein, do not worry that you yourself cannot be reborn there.
Even those ten types of evil and mad persons are all children of the Buddha; you should mindfully recite the Buddha's name and return home early.
If you do not seek refuge in your true, compassionate Father, you shall not escape the single iron blow from Ox-Head.
The myriad affairs of the world must be scrutinized with care; how could one avoid appearing before King Yama?
I have heard only that the Buddha possesses extraordinary skillful means, capable of delivering sentient beings from the realm of death.

I pray for an early rebirth in the Pure Land. My vow says:
"I suffer from toothache; what is the cause? Surely it must be because in a previous life I committed the grave transgression of slandering the Triple Gem, the Dharma, and the Sangha.
To this, I have added the further sin of slandering the Buddha—this offense is difficult to describe."
If one does not repent and make vows, One will surely fall into hell, where the suffering is most profound.
Therefore, burn six or eight incense sticks as an offering to the arm, To the Great Compassionate Honored One, Amitābha.
May I swiftly be freed from the agony of the toothache; May I shorten my lifespan here and be born early in the Pure Land.
May I soon behold the face of Amitābha; With words of truth, may I benefit all sentient beings.

Praising the Buddha and the Sangha with tireless heart, And further praising the wondrous Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, May I cause all beings to attain liberation; Only then shall my vows be fulfilled as I desire.
I look up with aspiration to the Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time, To all Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of worthy and holy Sangha.

May your great kindness and great compassion together bear witness, And may you equally grant protection and rescue, so that the long-standing vows Of those suffering in the realms of transmigration may be fulfilled.
In the year of Guiyou (1933), on the fifth day of the third lunar month, Gu Kun was stricken with a grave illness that persisted until autumn.

His nights were restless, his mouth would not open to take food, and he knew not what awaited him regarding the matter of life and death. Reflecting upon this life of mine, I have been capable of nothing else;
I have only placed my utmost faith in the single gateway of the Pure Land. Yet, I fear deeply that my past karma is profound and heavy, manifesting...
If one cannot fulfill one's aspirations while alive, is this not to betray the Buddha’s kindness?
To wear the dharma robes in vain and to waste all offerings made by those with faith—under the Buddha’s *kāṣāya*, to lose the human body—is most truly lamentable.

That one fails to accomplish the path within these extraordinary skillful means (upāya) is surely a cause for sorrow. Therefore, on the twenty-third day of the ninth month, [I spoke] according to the Tiantai teachings and contemplations.
The forty-nine-day period of seven weeks was inaugurated. Speech was strictly prohibited, and no one dared to be negligent.
Every morning, they reverently burned three sticks of arm-incense as an offering to Amitābha Buddha, making this vow:
The King of the Sixty-Eight Great Vows, With the wondrous power of compassion in its nine grades, May you cause me to quickly return and swiftly come to deliver all beings.
If my life-span has not yet ended, I vow that my illness shall be extinguished;
I shall resolve to exert diligent effort, Holding your name without ceasing.
Jièshù Fāyuàn Gǔkūn writes with shame:
For several years now, I have erroneously composed verses; I myself was unaware of their ugliness until I reflected upon them in stillness of mind.
Not only have I wasted my efforts entirely without benefit, but I have also exhausted my spirit and increased my deluded views.
The harm [of such pursuits] is no small matter. *Zhi guan* states: "To grasp and memorize [doctrines] exhausts the mind and weary the will;

to engage in the exchange of discourse muddies the water and clouds the pearl. While grasping and memorizing is indeed a vital task in studying the Buddha-dharma, even practitioners of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* must abandon it;
how much more so for those who single-mindedly hold the Name and seek birth in the present life—how could they afford to practice external studies that cause such disturbance?
It disturbs the mind and prevents the attainment of samādhi; rebirth [in the Pure Land] becomes difficult to secure. To rectify these former errors, he again composed a verse, saying:
"In vain I have composed verses to study external teachings, Falsely attracting worthy scholars to treat me with contempt. The Patriarchs' wondrous scriptures are piled as high as mountains;
What need is there for my blind self to engage in so much fabrication? How shameful! How shameful! Truly shameful! I have privately plucked the words of others to..."
Possessing such a deranged mind, he was unwilling to cease; the direct road to the West became a circuitous run.

As I repeatedly sought to restrain this profound obstruction, I found the horse of the mind difficult to halt. Therefore, in the same year of the *guǐyǒu* cycle, on the day the Buddha attained enlightenment, I [acted].
He reverently burned three incense sticks from his arm and made this vow: "If I, Gu Kun, should again compose verses in this life, I shall surely fall into hell.
He then reverently burned six more incense sticks from his arm as an offering to Śākyamuni Tathāgata and the World-Honored One Amitābha, praying:
"I only beseech you to bestow your compassionate power upon me, enabling me to concentrate my mind on the Buddha and swiftly proceed to the Western Land."
May you behold the Compassionate Honored One early on and suddenly open the Buddha-wisdom; may you preach the Dharma to benefit sentient beings throughout the limits of the future.

Regarding the earnest and fervent making of vows, Chan Master Miaoye said: "In friendship, do not seek what benefits oneself. If one seeks what benefits oneself, one will surely lose the way and righteousness. To lose [the way]...

The Way and its virtue necessarily involve seeing the faults of others. It is further said: "In dealing with others, do not seek their compliance or satisfaction. If others are compliant and satisfied, they will inevitably become self-conceited within;
being self-conceited within, they will surely cling to the notion that they alone are right. Consequently, Kun frequently delights in arbitrarily altering the words of his fellow students.

Is it not because one perceives the faults of others while clinging to one’s own correctness? Thus we know that when the Way is impaired by internal self-conceit, the harm received is no slight matter.
With pure karma yet unaccomplished, one cannot even save oneself; how then dare one judge the right and wrong of others? Such a person is truly possessed by a mad demon.

Reflecting upon this, he was filled with remorse that never ceased. Therefore, in the summer of the first year of the Guangxu era, he reverently burned nine incense sticks from his own arm before Amitābha Buddha in order to seek repentance. The verse of his vow reads:

Deeply ashamed of my lack of wisdom that gave rise to such deluded views, I have repeatedly and foolishly attempted to alter the words of my spiritual friend. Now, before the Buddha, I seek repentance;
may this madness be removed and I be swiftly reborn in the Lotus Land.
The *Essential Explanation of the Vows for the Seven Periods* states: "Whether one attains rebirth or not depends entirely on the presence or absence of faith and aspiration;

the high or low level of one's spiritual rank depends entirely on the depth or shallowness of one's recitation of the Name. Chewu says: "If one can truly give rise to the vow, faith is inherent within it. Once faith and aspiration are present..."

When these are complete, practice arises spontaneously without being sought. Therefore, among the three types of provisions—faith, aspiration, and practice—it is the single word "aspiration" that encompasses them all.
I, Kun, have always considered my own obstacles to be heavy; I must rely upon "single-mindedness without distraction" before I can attain rebirth.
In this present life, it is certainly impossible [to achieve birth]. If one can rely on faith and aspiration to be born there, it may be possible to exert effort.

Therefore, whenever establishing a seven-day retreat period, one must definitely take the recitation of one hundred thousand names of Amitābha as the daily practice to serve as the foundation for making vows; one must by no means seek "single-mindedness without distraction.
Every morning, one must inevitably offer three incense sticks with the arm extended as an offering to the Buddha, and with a sincere heart, make the following vow:
I now burn this arm-incense as an offering to Amitābha Buddha. I vow that at the end of my life, I shall certainly be reborn in that land.

As stated in the *Compassionate Cloud Repentance and Vow Ritual* (*Heqi yugai ciyun chan yuan yi*): "One must resolutely undertake pure karma so that it may be accomplished immediately; one must not harbor a single thought of attachment."

Regarding the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), one should censure and eliminate craving and desire; one should diligently still anger and delusion. Practitioners each possess beginningless evil habits;

they must swiftly seek to abandon them so that these do not become obstacles to correct repentance. One should observe which habit is most predominant, then censure, discard, and balance it, taking up the practice until it is restored to equilibrium.
Do not let the Dharma-practice be wasted in vain. For this purpose, I have extracted [the following] from the *Zhiguan Fandong* (Expedient Means of Calming and Contemplation).
I have composed ten verses based on the passage that rebukes the five desires and exhorts the abandonment of the five hindrances, appending to it my own aspiration for the Pure Land.
I have transcribed them by my seat to serve as a daily reminder to myself.
The various forms of sensual desire invade people with profound calamity; as they transmigrate through the six realms, their suffering increases ever more.
I pray that that Buddha will grant his compassionate pity, swiftly emitting light to receive us into rebirth there.
Seductive voices and艳丽 (yànqǔ) melodies are the sounds of manifold evils; they disturb practitioners so that the Way cannot be accomplished.
I vow to recite the Buddha’s name to be born in that land, where I shall constantly hear the numinous birds singing their profound tones.

The fragrance is so rich and pervasive that its harm is no small matter; even those of lofty aspirations are beset by it. I only pray that you will soon ascend to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing, where you shall awaken to non-arising amidst the scent of lotuses.
The śrāmaṇera Mi tasted flavors so excessively that he fell into the body of an insect; this desire has brought harm from time immemorial and its damage is profound.
Practice the path early to be reborn in Sukhāvatī, where exquisite food like *sūda* will manifest spontaneously.
Its touch is worthy of admiration, yet few know it brings so little harm; its defiled nature constantly craves fine, soft garments. Resting upon a lotus pedestal, its body is pure and clean;
when a gentle breeze brushes against it, the wonder is inconceivable.
When a greedy mind arises, all becomes dark and gloomy; human form is instantly transformed into the shape of a hungry ghost. Quickly recite the name of Amitābha to be born in the Treasure Land;
its enjoyments are manifest and ready for use, requiring no seeking.

Anger blazes fiercely; the fire of anger is like the form of a serpent. It incinerates the boundless forest of merit. From afar, I envy the virtuous friends in the Land of Bliss, who through loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity benefit all living beings.
The demon of sloth has long dwelt in the dark forest, constantly deceiving practitioners day and night. Vigorously鞭策 (urge) your body and mind while reciting the name of that Buddha;
return early to Sukhāvatī, and only then will there be peace and security.

Restlessness and regret are profound obstacles to body and mind; further entangled by sorrow and remorse, the Path will be difficult to accomplish. A single utterance of the Buddha’s name transcends birth and death;
such sovereign ease and leisure is beyond compare.

Doubt and the hindrance of doubt entangle the path so that it cannot be perfected; you must swiftly abandon them without harboring them in your mind. The road to the Land of Bliss is fundamentally close at hand;
only through the utmost faith can one easily attain rebirth there.

In the early summer of the Ren-shen year of the Tongzhi era, while at Jingjiao Jangsi Temple, Kun watched as Master Xianming was ill. He saw ten poems on a "Blood Image" (a blood-written Buddha image) composed by Dharma Master Miaoneng,
and rejoiced that they profoundly captured the principles of delighting in the wholesome and loathing the unwholesome, and of adopting and rejecting.

The meaning is profound. Therefore, disregarding my own mediocrity and folly, I have studied and harmonized with it. Each time I obtain two verses, I record them separately according to their original rhyme.
For a long time I have been estranged from Amitābha, the Great Teacher; I am submerged in the bitter sea of suffering and cannot escape.
I would cut open my body to paint an image of his compassion, shedding blood instead of fresh ink as tears fall.
With blood, I paint my Great Gracious Teacher of Sukhāvatī; for the rest of my life, I take refuge and dare not depart from you.
Drifting in the sea of suffering with no way out, I pray that you will extend your precious hand and reach down toward me.
Speaking thus of the gateway of death, tears drenched his face; deeply ashamed of having lived in vain, he could find no way to pursue the path.
With his very lifeblood, he painted an image of the Tathāgata, vowing: "May I swiftly hear the voice of Sukhāvatī."
The destitute child sighs in sorrow, tears streaming down; grieving over the lost *maṇi* jewel, he searches everywhere for its trace.
He sheds his own blood to paint a likeness of the Great Elder, seeking day by day for the descent of his great compassionate voice.
Toiling and striving, I have achieved nothing at all; I have betrayed the single point of clarity within my own spirit.
Relying on Amitābha’s compassionate reception, I reverently paint this blood image, vowing to seek rebirth there.

Virtuous deeds are difficult to accomplish while evil is easily formed; this is entirely due to the lack of clarity regarding cause and effect. Now, by carving out my tongue and using its blood to paint an image of the Compassionate One, I shall surely attain rebirth in the Nine Grades of the Lotus Pond.

At the time of committing karma, there is but a single body; yet in suffering through the three miserable realms, there are a thousand variations. May I be reborn from this world in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī);
with blood from my own veins, I shall carve out the likeness of that Buddha.
It is said that the holy and the ordinary each have but one body; who knows that the essence of true nature is without distinction? With sincere heart, paint an image of Amitābha;
it brings forth the model of the sun and moon within oneself.

The essence of awakening is numinous and luminous, inherently at peace; its measure encompasses the dharma-realm within the tip of a single hair. The sacred images on blood-stained diagrams all arise from this;
I only pray that all people will look with clear eyes.
The Adorned Pure Land is most worthy of peace; jeweled trees layer upon layer, their joys manifold.
Having painted an image of the Tamer from my own blood, I vow to be born in that land and gaze upon it from the balustrade.
Wandering through birth and death, coming and going in saṃsāra—on what day shall you ascend the terrace of the seven treasures? Cut your flesh and draw the Teacher to seek deliverance from suffering;
do not let your wailing cries resound like thunder.
He slit his own body and dripped his blood to paint the Tathāgata. May I, at the moment of death, ascend the precious terrace; may all Buddhas appear before me and extend their hands to me together.
Their Brahma-voices, consoling and encouraging, resound like thunder.
The single thought-moment before us is fundamentally alert; it is only through being defiled by external conditions that one loses one's own numinous spirit.
The Amitābha of blood-painting reveals his entire body; he is the Buddha of the mind, not a mere painting.
The ocean of Amitābha’s vows is tranquil yet ever-awake; it gathers in all sentient beings to restore their original numinous nature.
Carved from blood and painted into a true image—this mind is the Buddha, this is the brushwork.

The Buddha-nature eternally abides, neither old nor new; sentient beings, deluded and turning their backs on it, identify with this decaying body. With sincere devotion, they paint images of the Compassionate Honored One with blood;
may all living beings universally transcend defilement and dust.
A single spark of spiritual light is ever-new for all eternity. When the root of emotion covers and obscures it, one becomes an ordinary body.
To paint a Buddha of the Western Land upon a heart stained with blood—may this resolve exhaust the dust of kalpas throughout the Sahā world.
The shackles of passion and the chains of craving cannot be opened; quickly turn back and plant the lotus roots.
Facing the West with reverence, he sheds the blood from his tongue, painting that Buddha so that He appears as if truly present.
That Buddha’s gate of vows stands wide open; one should swiftly cultivate the seeds of faith. I have now painted this image of the Golden Pond with my own blood;
it remains clearly within my heart, without coming or going.
Chasing after illusions through vast eons, I have lost my true nature; In deep sorrow, I see my life passing in vain, betraying my compassionate parents.
Now I take this vow to uphold the Name, Dropping blood to attest my sincerity and painting the Buddha’s form.
To transcribe the name of Amitābha is itself the One True Reality; only when one is personally willing will one truly become intimate with it.
You must further take this as your foundation to escape birth and death, never forgetting the body of that Buddha in every thought-moment.

Sealing the niche for his friend, he lifted the seal and said: "Within the realm of True Suchness (Tathatā), there is fundamentally no separation between east and west; yet within the gate of birth and extinction, there nevertheless appear the forms of coming and going.
We reverently pay homage to the Venerable Master Xianming of Jingantang, whose lifelong practice was perfected and whose Great Matter [was realized]."
Perfected and complete, it may be said that he comes from nowhere; having been born here in the Eastern Land, he likewise goes nowhere.

As he departs for the Western Paradise, I offer these few words once more to briefly express my reverence for his noble virtue. Having left the mundane world and distanced himself from the dust of defilement for several decades, he sought teachers and inquired after the Way with a vast and profound resolve.
When the conditions were ripe, the flower of his mind blossomed, and he personally beheld the original host of non-arising. He has applied himself to Zen meditation with arduous dedication.

His merit was already perfected; forgetting his own body for the sake of the multitude, he became even more diligent. Day by day he performed a hundred tasks without weariness; sitting at night to contemplate the mind, he reached the fifth watch.
His observance of the precepts was as pure as snow; through compassion and patience, he benefited all living beings. When speaking, he did not mention the faults of others;
dwelling in the world, he always maintained a mind of detachment from it. At the moment of death, he had no lingering concerns—only...
Meditate on Amitābha and aspire for rebirth in the Pure Land. It is fortunate that Master Xian has returned to the West; it is truly lamentable that we have few who understand us.
Now tell me: what is the single phrase for sealing the coffin? "Many years of arduous practice were as frantic as a speeding arrow;
today, at ease, he sits upon the precious lotus. Then, seal it.

For those who practice *nenbutsu* with the intent of attaining rebirth in the Pure Land, the most feared thing at the time of death is harboring doubt and becoming discouraged within themselves, thinking:
"We are ordinary beings caught in the cycle of birth and death; our karmic obstructions are so profound—how could we possibly attain rebirth in this single lifetime? All such thoughts are incorrect.

Just as by the power of Amitābha’s vows, this skillful means was specifically established for the sake of delivering suffering sentient beings so that they may achieve accomplishment in a single lifetime.

The *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "Even those who have committed the ten evil acts or the five heinous crimes, when oppressed by suffering at the moment of death, are taught to recite the ten recitations;
they shall immediately be born in that land. Is this not a clear proof of accomplishment in a single lifetime? The ten evil acts and the five heinous crimes are, indeed, the greatest...
Even a person of great evil can achieve success in this very life; how much more so for one of minor evil, or one who is without evil?
How much more so for one who has practiced the recitation of the Buddha's name throughout their entire life—how could such a person not certainly attain rebirth? A doubter says:

"Those of great evil who recite the Buddha's name at the moment of death and attain rebirth through ten recitations must all possess deep and profound roots of goodness from past lives; it is only because of this that they are able to do so. The commentary says: "Great..."
Even for an evil person, there still remain roots of goodness from past lives; how much more so for those who commit minor evils? How much more so for those who commit no evil?

And how much more so for those who have recited the Buddha’s name throughout their lives—how could it be possible for them to lack roots of goodness? One should know that it is simply a matter of encountering a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra).
Those who hear the name of the Buddha are all people whose roots of goodness from past lives are profound and deep;
they must not harbor doubts within themselves or obstruct their own minds, thereby allowing this single life to pass in vain with no accomplishment in the path.

I have personally seen virtuous friends whose faculties were most sharp and whose meritorious practices were transcendent, yet who failed to attain rebirth because they harbored doubts at the time of death. Conversely, there were those who were dull-witted and simple, yet who were sincere...
By reciting the Buddha’s name at the time of death, one will immediately attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

It can be seen that regarding the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, it does not matter whether one's spiritual capacity is great or small, nor the depth of one's meritorious practice; provided one has deep faith in the Buddha’s words, all shall achieve success.
Thus, the Patriarch Cizhao said: "I thought that as an ordinary person, I could not be born in the Pure Land; therefore, I personally maintained the fasts and precepts, vowing for the future life."
As human beings, one must practice the path through successive stages before being able to be born in that land. I have seen many practitioners who constantly speak in such a way;
they do not accord with the vows of Amitābha nor the sutras of the Pure Land. Their minds are shrouded by false views, and thus it is ultimately difficult for them to attain liberation.
This is not the obstruction of others; it is entirely the obstruction of their own minds. Failing to be born in this life, they will miss the opportunity once and for all.
Hundred-fold errors! I exhort you, O practitioners, to believe the words spoken by the Tathāgata. The Buddha never speaks anything that is not true; how could these be empty or deceptive words?
You should simply be diligent for yourselves and seek the Pure Land with a single-minded focus.

In the winter of the Gengwu year, while I was at Jingjiao Temple undertaking a seven-day *nianfo* retreat under the compassionate protection of the Buddha’s grace, I contracted a minor illness. Consequently, I became weary and unable to maintain my practice;
my mind began to wander with random thoughts. Suddenly, I recalled the times when I lived at home and provided for my own food and clothing.

It is difficult to plan for; suffering is beyond words. Now, by the grace of the Buddha, all matters have been brought to completion. Yet, if I fall even slightly ill, how could I bear to be negligent?
Having encountered such a favorable opportunity as this, if I do not again apply myself with diligence to the recitation of the Buddha’s name, when will there ever be an end to my suffering?
Consequently, I suddenly felt refreshed; my spirit became clear and my breath invigorated. My recitation of the Buddha’s name appeared to gain considerable power.
Thus, I composed four verses on wearying of suffering, leaving home, reciting the Buddha’s name, and seeking rebirth [in the Pure Land], which I used to constantly admonish myself.

I reproach myself for the deep roots of my transgressions accumulated over kalpas; my retribution lies in being born into a poor family as one who endures bitter toil. Food and clothing are difficult to secure, and I am beset by many hardships;

I have no one among my neighbors to rely upon, which is most distressing. Though I possess some skills and crafts, they are empty and tasteless. Fortunately, through the occasion of illness, a mind of renunciation has arisen.
Moved by the Buddha’s compassion, he has extended his protection; I vow to cultivate the Great Practice to deliver all living beings.
A foolish person who committed evil has suddenly become a monk; I know not what causes from the past have led to this. To encounter sweet rain during a drought is no mere blessing of mine;

to meet a skilled physician while ill is the merit of the Sage. As a great stone about to sink does not yet drown, and a heavy prisoner facing death is granted life—may I pray for swift deliverance from the suffering of saṃsāra, and through extensive study of Bodhi, repay the Buddha’s kindness.
Fortunate to have become a monk, distinct from the worldly crowd; yet I am deeply ashamed that my defilements are heavy and the Way is difficult to accomplish.
Delusive thoughts arise in turmoil within my breast, and greed and anger in my mind never cease for a moment. Having begun to study the Chan school, my conditions have not yet matured;

wishing to cultivate the Pure Land practice, illness has assailed me. Alas! The precious realm remains empty and unattained; thus I make a vow to single-mindedly recite the names of the One of Ten Thousand Virtues.

I vow to recite the Buddha’s name until the end of my life, establishing a daily discipline of sixty thousand recitations morning after morning. Rebirth [in the Pure Land] depends entirely upon the resolve of single-minded cultivation;

wandering through the realms of transmigration arises solely from a heedless mind. The people of Sukhāvatī all attain non-retrogression, whereas even the wealthy and noble of Saṃsāra may sink into ruin.
I seek only to be entrusted early to the depths of the lotus pond, so as to avoid suffering within the wheel of misery in Jambudvīpa.
In the winter of the Gengwu year during our joint administration, while I was at Jingjiao Temple, I had one scroll of the Six-Character Great Name mounted and enshrined within my quarters.
On the day it was first hung, I knelt with all my strength and recited it a thousand times to express my sincere devotion. Suddenly, I recalled the Ten Thousand Virtues.
The Great Name. The grace of saving my dying heart caused my voice and tears to emerge involuntarily, and so I composed this verse:
"The six characters of the Great Name are wondrous beyond measure; All boundless merits are contained within them. Our Original Teacher proclaimed them again and again for our sake;
All Buddhas have taught them everywhere because of this. Shandao invoked them many times and emitted many rays of light; Shaokang chanted them once and [emitted] one..."
Flying Buddha. I now kneel and recite, remembering your profound kindness; with every phrase and every sound, tears flow forth together.

The *Qingling Zhijie Mituo Yaoyie* (The Joyful Reception of the Direct and Expedient Essential Explanation of Amitābha) states: "Amitābha Buddha is the great name of myriad virtues. To invoke virtue by means of the name, there is nothing that is not fully present."
It is not exhausted. Chan Master Chewu said: "The single phrase of the Buddha one recollects is established as a name based entirely upon virtue;

there is no name apart from virtue, for the name is invoked by virtue. There is no virtue apart from the name, for virtue is entrusted to the name. I address those who practice the recitation of the name:

you should contemplate these words, for only then will you know that reciting the name does not require visualizing the Buddha's form. It is the most simple, easy, direct, and immediate method. I feel ashamed that over the past few years...
Failing to understand this essential point, they follow the lead of clever people and falsely claim that the name of Amitābha is intended only for those of inferior capacity.
They maintain that if one of superior intelligence practices *nianfo*, one must investigate and cultivate visualization (*guan*) to truly possess both Chan and Pure Land.

Constantly harboring this view, they ultimately fail to reach the depths of investigation through their investigations, nor do they achieve success in their visualizations. Fortunately, during the year of Xin...

Before even spring arrives, one attains the understanding that enters into the virtue of Amitābha’s three bodies; by constantly invoking his name, it is suddenly manifested. The *Yuánzhōng chāo* states:

"A single invocation of his auspicious title causes ten thousand virtues to manifest simultaneously. If such a marvel truly exists, from this point on, through observation and contemplation, the mind reaches its cessation.

I am filled with the utmost joy and gratitude. Had it not been for the diligent toil of my parents, who taught me to read for two years and recognize a few characters, how could there be this present day?
I feel ashamed that since leaving the household life, I have had no means to offer them in return; therefore, I have lit forty-eight incense sticks from my own arm as an offering to Amitābha Buddha.
I pray that my biological parents may, by virtue of these roots of goodness, be reborn early in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Thus, he composed a verse:
"By means of the name, the root of virtue is invoked; the Buddha is clearly present within one's mouth.
If one attains the holding of the name without other thoughts, every sound reveals the countenance of purple-gold."
Holding the prayer beads and reciting the Buddha’s name, the Buddha within the beads is most clearly manifest.
Yet, because one's own karmic conditions are heavy, its form remains unseen throughout the entire day.

My family is poor, yet I have already studied books for two years. My parents have labored with sweat falling like rain. Now that I am able to be summoned by name to serve Emperor Dezong, it relies entirely upon my ability to read characters and contemplate the words of the scriptures.
Upon my arms, I reverently burn the sixty-eight incenses, making offerings to Amitābha Buddha with a sincere heart.
By this merit, I pray that my parents may swiftly escape the wheel of suffering and be reborn in the Land of Bliss.
Regretting my former errors and excesses,
I lament how I once fell into the one-sided emptiness; I falsely claimed to have clarified the supreme lineage, while fixating on Amitābha with a bland indifference,
yet boasting of a profound and flourishing realization of the ground.

When I first left the household life, I originally believed in the Western [tradition]. At first I rejoiced in the principles of Chan, yet I secretly resented its lowliness. Only upon encountering the calamity of war did I realize my error;
I have completely revised all my previous misconceptions.

Those of the Pure Land school who have not yet entered it claim to be "Universal" (Tong); they give a confused interpretation of Amitābha as being their own master. Though they recite the Great Name, I am pleased by their mindfulness;
yet within their hearts, they remain attached to the distinction between "here" and "there."

I studied reverent worship and understood only emptiness; I mistakenly claimed that a pure mind was itself the Lotus Palace. Only upon reading the *Ten Essentials* did I clearly perceive the West, whereupon I finally resolved to uphold the practice of reciting the Name and vowed to abandon the East.
The Name and Original Vow:
Sentient beings have heavy defilements and the Path is difficult to cultivate; the sea of suffering is vast and boundless—how can one emerge from it? For this reason, Dharmakara established his vows:
"I shall deliver the multitudes solely by means of my Name."
The Name of Amitābha is a boundless vow; it universally gathers in the ordinary and the ignorant, sudden and complete.
When the wicked and rebellious turn their hearts for but ten recitations, the fiery chariots are transformed into purple-gold lotuses.
Holding the name, one naturally attains the Great Name;

it resonates faintly as it is recited from within the mouth. With hands counting the beads of the *mālā*, listen with tranquil stillness. Listening, you hear the profound sound clearly and distinctly;
it is as if a Buddha were suddenly manifesting his true body.
Parting his lips, he recites the Buddha’s name in a faint murmur; Drawing in his ears and clarifying his mind, he listens with subtle attention.
